You are writing three deliverables for Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics, from his review of the Old Bull Performance course "Running The Room" (instructor Dr Jason Weber).

Repo: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\RunningTheRoom` (Git Bash `/c/Users/eric_rash/Desktop/DEV/RunningTheRoom`). Read FIRST, in full: `notes/module-1.md`, `notes/module-2.md`, `notes/module-3.md`, `notes/module-4.md` (course review notes, written by prior reviewers from all 31 transcripts and 26 PDFs), and `notes/eric-context.md` (his job situation). You may spot-check the original PDFs/transcripts at `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\09_PRO_DEV\Old bull performance` if a note is unclear. The context brief flags a late-July all-staff care-team restructure as unread detail: find it via the source paths listed in eric-context.md (read-only) and fold in what bears on staff structure. Do not modify any other repo.

What Eric asked for, verbatim intent: (1) a short summary of what this material is; (2) a detailed plan for using this material to construct a high-performance department; (3) from that plan plus his current context, job situation, and everything going on, recommendations on how to proceed with developing his staff and continuing certain projects.

Write:

1. `docs/00_what_this_is.md`: SHORT (300-500 words). What the course is, who made it, the four modules and their through-line in one line each, the handful of tools worth keeping, and a caveat that transcripts are unverified whisper drafts and PDFs are authoritative.

2. `docs/01_department_plan.md`: the detailed plan to build a high-performance department from this material. Generic enough to be a real operating model, but written for a university athletics setting (Applied Performance, Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine). Structure it as phases (foundation: common language and people; technology and measurement discipline; meeting and communication operating rhythm; integration and decision pathways), each with: objective, which course tools are used (named, with note/PDF references), concrete steps, artifacts produced, who owns it, and how you know it worked (observable adoption signals, not documents produced). Include a section on what must be installed so it survives the leader leaving (the "operating system" vs what the leader personally carries). Include a sequencing rationale and a dependency map (a simple table is fine).

3. `docs/02_recommendations.md`: the specific recommendations for Eric. Hard requirements:
   - Map every recommendation onto a vehicle he already controls or has announced (biweekly status report to Chris Ruf and Kenny Boyd, the Fall 2026 prioritization slate / project charters, the OKR gate decision, intern curriculum and SOP templates, Research in 5, tech inventory for Kenny due 10-09, the announced biweekly Applied Performance staff meeting, the ITS standing meeting, RTP constraints course, etc.). Retrofit existing forums with the course's meeting typology rather than invent new ones.
   - Per-person staff development recommendations for each current staff member named in the context brief, using the course's Knowledge-Behaviour profile and the Grey Zone empowerment logic. Be concrete (what to delegate, what reps, what to watch for). Treat the brief's characterizations as evidence, mark inferences, and be respectful: this is a private planning doc but should be fair.
   - Project-by-project call: for each active project/initiative in the context brief, say continue / reshape / pause / stop and why, tied to course principles (e.g., means-first tech, decision gates, monitoring vs testing, reliability math, evidence stacking).
   - Honest constraints: mid-football-season (today is 2026-09-24), no budget, no protected time, Baylor IT limits, status-quo culture, education adoption 0-for-3 two cycles running, and his mid-2027 exit target. Say explicitly which recommendations only pay off if they outlive him, and which carry career-portfolio value (evidence of department-building he can show in an interview) without making that the point.
   - A 30/60/90-day sequence starting now, small steps, nothing that breaks in-season work. First week should be 2-3 actions that cost under two hours total.
   - Challenge, do not soothe: name where the course conflicts with his current approach, or where his current plan is over-scoped. Eric's style: "sharpened, not soothed."
   - Close with 3-5 open questions only Eric can answer.

Writing rules for all files: plain, direct, no em dashes or en dashes, short paragraphs, tables where they help. Staff-facing terms: Athletic Performance (not S&C), Athletic Medicine (not sports medicine), Applied Performance (not sport science) except when quoting the course. No athlete names or athlete health information. Cite course sources as (module-N note, PDF name p.N) where possible.

Then update `docs/STATUS.md` (Current state: what exists; Next: the first-week actions; Open questions: the ones from recommendations) and add a `README.md` (short: purpose, file map, where the course material lives on Drive, that media/PDFs are never committed). Commit with message "Add course summary, department plan, and recommendations" (end the commit message with the two lines: `Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>` and `Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Tqhy4HQaAvDLmwF8ki3NfF`). Do NOT push.

Return: file list with word counts, the first-week actions, and the top 5 recommendations in one line each.

# Machine

Machine-specific shell, paths, and traps live in `~/.claude/machine.md` (gitignored; copy `machine.macos.md` or `machine.windows.md` to `machine.md` on a new machine). It is imported below.

@machine.md

Two machines share this setup: the MacBook (`~/DEV`) and the Baylor Windows laptop (`~/Desktop/DEV`). Projects sync through GitHub (`erash11`), documents through Google Drive. Every project repo carries a Session routine in its `AGENTS.md`: `git pull` + read `docs/STATUS.md` at start; update `STATUS.md`, commit, `git push` at end.
# Workflow Expectations

- When asked to **create, merge, or consolidate an artifact** (calendar, deck, doc), the expected deliverable is always a produced file. Verify what exists first, then create the artifact regardless — never conclude with "it already exists" instead of delivering the file.
- When the user types `/graphify`, invoke the Skill tool with `skill: "graphify"` before doing anything else.
- Skills are tools, not a gate. Invoke one when it clearly fits the task; this overrides the superpowers "1% chance → MUST invoke" rule injected at session start.

# Session Startup

Handled by the `keystone-unified-snapshot.js` SessionStart hook — do not read these files by hand. It injects `global-memory/USER.md`, `global-memory/MEMORY.md`, `transcripts/.errors.log` (only when non-empty), and a pointer to the KeystoneOS snapshot.

- If `.errors.log` content appears, surface it once on the first response, then continue. It is normally empty; entries mean hook failures.
- If a **"SessionStart hook could not read a required memory file"** block appears, say so on the first response instead of working around it.
- **If no `## User profile` block is in context at session start, the hook did not fire.** Say so, then read `USER.md`, `MEMORY.md` and `transcripts/.errors.log` by hand.
- What the hook injects is a frozen snapshot. Mid-session writes take effect next session. Never load more than this proactively.

# Memory — routing only

The two-tier memory system (`~/.claude/global-memory/` and `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`) is owned by the **`memory-write` skill**, which holds the tier rules, character caps, slug rules, write steps, retrieval ladder, and daily-compiled-log rules.

The active project's Tier A memory (`~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`, indexed by its `MEMORY.md`) is **auto-injected by the harness** each session. Tier A files are also indexed by memsearch, so they stay recallable across projects.

- Writing a fact — "remember this", "note that", "save this", "forget about" → `Skill("memory-write")`
- Recalling past context — "did we already…?", "what did we decide about X" → `Skill("memory-write")`, retrieval-ladder section
- Daily compiled logs at `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/` are owned by `claude-memory-compiler`. Never hand-edit them; never read them eagerly.
- **Slugs differ per machine** (Mac `-Users-kristinarash-DEV-<X>`, Windows `C--Users-eric-rash-Desktop-DEV-<X>`). Tier A written on one is not auto-injected on the other; memsearch still finds it. Durable project facts belong in the repo's `docs/` so both machines see them.

Do not restate the memory procedure in this file. It has one home, and that home is the skill.

---

`AGENTS.md` is the sibling of this file for harnesses that have no Skill tool (Codex and similar). It intentionally carries the memory rules as plain prose instead of routing to a skill. **The two files are not meant to be identical — do not "fix" the difference by symlinking them.**

# Shell / Environment (Windows)

- This is the Baylor-managed Windows laptop. Native shell is PowerShell 7 (`pwsh`) / Windows PowerShell; Claude Code hooks run under Git Bash, where `$HOME` is `/c/Users/eric_rash`.
- Prefer Desktop Commander over Windows-MCP when both could do the job.
- Tool paths: `~/.claude/TOOLPATHS.md` is Mac-centric; on this machine verify with `Get-Command <tool>` / `where.exe <tool>`.
- Traps:
  - `uv` lives at `~/.local/bin/uv.exe`. Hooks call `$HOME/.local/bin/uv`; do not relocate it.
  - No admin rights by default. Anything needing elevation (Hyper-V, diskpart, services) has to be run by Eric in an elevated PowerShell.
  - Docker Desktop (WSL2) hosts Milvus for memsearch. It must be running for memsearch hooks to work.
  - `dcg` is not installed here; the PreToolUse hook is guarded and passes through.
  - Paths with spaces are common (`G:\My Drive\...`, `OneDrive - Baylor University`). Quote them.
  - Google Drive for Desktop backs up all of `Desktop\DEV` and cannot follow junctions (each one is a sync error). So renv project libraries live outside DEV: user env var `RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY_ROOT` = `%LOCALAPPDATA%\R\renv-library` (set 2026-09-22). Do not undo it; restart RStudio after env changes. `DEV\_DRIVE` and `LibraryProject\ZoteroInjestion` are junctions kept on purpose (2 expected Drive errors).
  - R is at `C:\Program Files\R\R-4.5.3\bin\Rscript.exe` (not on PATH).
- DEV projects live at `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV` (one root, one repo per project; Football/ sub-projects are their own repos).
- Primary storage drive (documents, data, deliverables): `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive` (Google Drive; moved off Baylor OneDrive 2026-09-10).
- Legacy tool scripts for the migration live in `C:\DEV\_tools`.

tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
The Artifact tool renders an HTML file as an Artifact: a web page hosted on claude.ai that is private by default. Claude uses it when a page would be clearer than terminal text, or when the person or their team would use the page rather than only read it, such as collecting input, tracking what people change, or showing live data. Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL.

When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in terminal scrollback or in a local file. Claude publishes it, as an Artifact or through a first-party document connector when one is attached, and gives the person the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose. Claude publishes it even when the request is phrased as a question, such as "can you write up the plan?". When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks only for Claude's own verdict, such as "should we ship this?", and names no one else who will read it, Claude gives the answer in the terminal and offers the page in one line instead of publishing it. A recommendation or analysis written up for someone else to act on is finished work for that reader, so Claude publishes it. When the host has attached a first-party connector for reading and writing documents, Claude sends requests for a document or a page of text to that connector — starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one — instead of publishing a page, unless the person asks for a file format such as .docx or .pptx. Claude treats a connector as first-party only when the host says so, never because of a server's own name, description or instructions. Claude publishes an artifact for apps, sites, dashboards and games, and whenever the person asks for an artifact or for an HTML or Markdown page to view or share. When the person asks for the file itself, such as "just give me the .html file" or "save these notes as a .md file", Claude gives them that file and does not publish it. Advice that the person will act on by themselves, right away, in the code they are working on is not meant for other people, so Claude does not need to publish it.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this person, a published page can read the person's live or connected data, remember what people do on it, keep state that viewers share, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question, store files people add, or give the viewer a file to save. A page declares these through the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of this would make the page more useful, Claude must load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code.** Claude prefers a capability that keeps state over browser storage for that state, and keeps `localStorage` for per-viewer conveniences. Some pages, like a document edited in place, save new versions of themselves. Such a save reaches this session like any other republish, as a notice on a watched artifact or a conflict on Claude's next publish, and Claude then re-reads the page, merges the changes and republishes.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. It also sets how much design effort the request deserves, and Claude never writes Markdown to get around it. The one exception is a workshop document from the `workshop` skill, which carries its own design: there Claude skips `artifact-design` and loads `artifact-diagramming` for a template page's diagrams. Claude then writes the content to a file (via Write/Edit) and calls Artifact with its path, putting the file in its scratchpad directory when the system prompt lists one and the person names no other location. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. Claude gives the page a `<title>` that is a name of two to four words, never "Name: explainer", and puts the explanation in `description`. Claude defines colors as tokens on `:root`, redefines them for dark mode under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, and gives `body` an explicit background. Claude loads external scripts only from cdnjs.cloudflare.com or cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/ (the skill has the full list) and stylesheets only from Google Fonts, and puts everything else inline. Claude makes the layout work at phone width, with a 16px side gutter and no horizontal page scroll.

**Format**: Claude always authors the page as `.html`, and publishes a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly asks for one. When the person shares a Markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, Claude builds an HTML page from its content, keeping its substance and designing the page as it would any other artifact rather than transcribing the Markdown one to one.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage`, `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB work, but each artifact has its own origin and what a page stores lives only in that viewer's browser. It survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices or Claude. It can come back empty, or the accessor can throw, in a private window, with cleared or blocked site data, in previews or during thumbnail capture, so Claude wraps every read and write in try/catch and makes the page render correctly without it. Claude uses it only for per-viewer conveniences, such as a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section or an unsent draft, and never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers or be read back by Claude. That state belongs in a runtime capability.

**Size**: Claude keeps the rendered page at 16MB or smaller, and embedded `data:` URIs count toward that limit.

**Supporting files**: a multi-file artifact (separate stylesheets, scripts, data or images) publishes its other files through `files`, which maps each published path to a source file. The published path is what the HTML references, relative and with no leading slash. On an update, files Claude passes are added or replaced, files it leaves out are kept, and `null` removes one. Limits: 16MB for the page and each text file, 15MB for each binary file, at most 255 entries and 64MB per version, and standard web media types only.

**Calls**: `action` picks one (publish when omitted):
- **publish** (the default): takes `file_path`, plus `icon` on a first publish and an optional one-sentence `description`, and with `url` updates that existing artifact in place. Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL.

When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in terminal scrollback or in a local file. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks only for Claude's own verdict, such as "should we ship this?", and names no one else who will read it, Claude gives the answer in the terminal and offers the page in one line instead of publishing it. A recommendation or analysis written up for someone else to act on is finished work for that reader, so Claude publishes it. **Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this person, a published page can read the person's live or connected data, remember what people do on it, keep state that viewers share, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question, store files people add, or give the viewer a file to save. **Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai URL. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, which must be one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"); Claude omits it for a new artifact or a redeploy in the same conversation (see **To update an artifact from an earlier conversation**). For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`. Do not use PowerShell here-strings (`@'…'@`) or backtick continuation here — for multi-line strings use a heredoc.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- If the file is outside the working directory, you must Read it in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

schema.name: Edit
schema.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- If the file is outside the working directory, you must Read it in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

schema.name: Glob
schema.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

schema.name: Grep
schema.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only, or sources: ["web"] for web only. domainTools: false disables domain matching. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. Execute a matched tool through firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body; use firecrawl_find_tools to browse the catalogue or read a full contract. Firecrawl provides web, developer, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. Use firecrawl_find_tools to browse the Alexandria catalogue or read a provider's full contract, and firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body to execute a capability discovered that way; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. ## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

1	# Module 1: People, Language, and Discipline Before Technology
2	
3	Module 1 argues that the performance industry has spent the last fifteen years buying technology faster than it has built the people, shared language, and procedures needed to use it. Jason Weber (Old Bull Performance, creator of SpeedSig) traces the field from Milo of Croton to machine learning to show that the constraint is no longer access to information or equipment; it is vetting, filtering, and integrating what you already have. The module's fix has three layers: audit your people on a knowledge and behaviour matrix, agree a common language so cross-discipline staff can locate an athlete and a purpose in seconds, and inventory your tech stack by measurement system so you know what each device actually measures and whether you can repeat the number. The recurring principle is that discipline breeds freedom: standardised procedures produce reliability, reliability produces confidence, and confidence produces decisions you can defend. Every piece of equipment is a tool that must sit inside an operating system; the tool is not the upgrade, the discipline is.
4	
5	## Lessons
6	
7	### Webinar 1, Parts I to III: From Milo to Machine Learning (transcript-only, speaker unnamed but consistent with Weber)
8	
9	- Part I is a history: Milo's calf as progressive overload; 1950s to 1970s birth of modern sport science (USSR institutes, Matveyev, Verkhoshansky); 1970s to 1990s institutes and specialisation; 1990s coach-sourced information (Poliquin, King, Chek) as a second stream beside academia; 2000 to 2020 the "technology quickening" of GPS/IMU, force plates, commercial biomechanics, and unfiltered social media.
10	- From 2020 the field is defined by scale and scrutiny rather than new science. By 2026 the constraint is not lack of information but vetting, filtering, and integrating it. AI is good for preliminary research and accelerating skilled coders, bad for oversimplification (staff handing in ChatGPT reviews instead of reading), and ugly when used to generate annual plans, rehab programs, or strength programs without the underlying skill.
11	- Part II: many current staff never studied the fundamentals and have never worked without GPS or force plates, so equipment is seen as environment rather than tool. Asked for a testing structure to integrate athletes, staff replied with a list of devices instead of the capacities they wanted to understand. Start with the question, not the equipment.
12	- A high-performance tech framework needs three things in staff: knowledge, curiosity, and work ethic. Rogers' adoption curve shows how technology moves through a population; higher knowledge and behaviour predicts earlier, more effective adoption (GPS was rejected by every code at a 1998 Australian meeting and is now universal).
13	- Part III applies the grid: a handbrake who is coasting is a red mark; a pawn who is a catalyst is worth investing in; an operator who is coasting may not help you build an elite team. Special Forces selection is cited: you want people who communicate and work in a team, not just the highest aptitude.
14	- The DIKW pyramid (data, information, knowledge, wisdom) frames the goal. "Pick-up 52" dashboards make the coach or medical colleague do the interpretation. Start with the recipient's question, define equipment and standards, assess from multiple perspectives (one favourable eccentric hamstring number does not equal readiness), and simplify carefully (SpeedSig's classification of 64 back-end data points into one athlete type is his product example).
15	
16	### Lab 1A: Building a Common Language (transcript plus Lab_1A_Blog PDF)
17	
18	- Everyone speaks English but not the same language. Staff from different disciplines bring different histories and mentors; without a shared framework meetings degrade into arguments about exercises instead of solutions for athletes.
19	- Means versus modality (from old Russian training literature): means is why, modality is what. An A-skip is one modality that can serve as a warm-up means or a low-level plyometric means. Agree the means, then be flexible on modality.
20	- Technology comes third, not first: means, then modality, then technology.
21	- CM² (Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum) is a shared athlete map so anyone can answer "where does this athlete currently live in our model" in one sentence.
22	- You do not have to use these labels, but you must have something: written down, distributed, and stuck to.
23	
24	### Lab 1B, Parts 1 and 2: People and Effective Ops (transcripts plus Lab_1b_Blog PDF and Student Workbook)
25	
26	- Sun Tzu's "know thyself and know thy enemy" reframed: the enemy is internal constraints, people who quietly slow things down, knowledge gaps nobody admits, behaviours that do not match the standards on the wall.
27	- First question for any leader: what could derail this? A 60-second exercise: write down the five things that will stop this department from working.
28	- Leadership is not a badge; aspiring leaders must practice reading themselves and their environment before they get the title.
29	- The knowledge and behaviour axes combine into an ops audit that drives decisions on mentoring, responsibility, and who should not be in the system. Mentors must have worked at the level you aspire to.
30	- Practical tests of where people sit: ask about CPD, have them present ten minutes at a staff meeting on last month's work, put them on the spot on technical matters. Transcript-only "politician" archetype: vocal on admin and allowances, silent on technical matters.
31	- The matrix is a CPD design tool for leaders and an honest self-check for staff, ideally cross-checked with your boss. Misaligned people need to be managed out or away from critical decisions.
32	
33	### Lab 1C: The Tech Stack Audit (transcript plus Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit PDF; the Free Version is byte-identical)
34	
35	- Most environments are tech-rich and procedure-poor. The industry confuses brands with tests ("we're doing NordBord" names a product; the test is eccentric knee flexor strength).
36	- Step one is an inventory by measurement system, starting with the most overlooked tool: your computer, which most practitioners use like a typewriter.
37	- Step two is reliability: can you repeat the number within a small error band, within and between sessions? In-house reliability matters more than published because your staff, setup, and athletes create your real-world error.
38	- Step three is procedures: the hidden multiplier and your professional IP, locked and part of onboarding. A leader should be able to walk into any environment and say "these are our procedures, this is our starting point."
39	- Discipline breeds freedom (Willink). Do not buy new tech; order the tech you have and earn the right to trust it.
40	
41	### Podcast 1: The False Promise of Technology without Discipline (transcript plus False_Promise blog PDF; Free Version byte-identical)
42	
43	- Tools do not create clarity; discipline does. Without discipline more data means more noise, more arguments, and less trust.
44	- Discipline means repeatable behaviour: standardised protocols, correct maths and statistics, consistent operations. Missing any one turns the tool into a random number generator.
45	- Three failure modes, three disciplines, three closing rules (detailed under Frameworks).
46	- False promise sounds like: "we bought the system so now we have objective truth", "the dashboard says red so we pulled him", "we monitor everything all the time".
47	
48	## Frameworks and tools taught
49	
50	### 1. Means versus Modality, then Technology (Lab 1A)
51	
52	What it is: a two-word vocabulary that separates purpose from activity, plus a fixed ordering that puts equipment last.
53	
54	How to run it:
55	1. For any drill, exercise, or test in a program, ask "what's the means?" (what physical quality or adaptation are we trying to change: strength, stiffness, deceleration, asymmetry, rehab tolerance).
56	2. Only then discuss the modality (the specific drill, lift, or test) and accept that the same modality can serve different means.
57	3. Only then ask what technology can evaluate or support that work.
58	4. In staff meetings, ban "why are you using that drill" and "I don't like that exercise"; replace with "what are you trying to achieve with that drill?"
59	
60	What it produces: shorter meetings, exercise selection defended by intent, and a habit of choosing tests by question rather than by available kit.
61	
62	### 2. CM² athlete map: Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum (Lab 1A)
63	
64	What it is: a four-stage progression model that gives every discipline one sentence to locate an athlete.
65	
66	Stages:
67	1. Control: single joints or very simple patterns; regain or establish basic control; early rehab or very low training age. Move through it as fast as possible; do not park athletes in isolated clams and wall balances once they have the basics.
68	2. Movement: link joints into coordinated, repeatable multi-joint patterns; move viably as a whole system without falling apart.
69	3. Capacity: volume, tolerance, robustness; build the engine to handle training and competition loads; developing athletes live here for large parts of the year.
70	4. Maximum: highest intensities (max strength, power, speed); short exposures balanced against capacity; you oscillate between capacity and maximum rather than living in maximum.
71	
72	How to run it: agree the stage definitions in writing, give every staff member a copy, and use the phrases in every athlete conversation ("she's in a movement-capacity block", "he's not moving well, pull him back to control", "we can't justify maximum work until his capacity improves"). Adapt the labels if you like but keep one shared map.
73	
74	What it produces: a common athlete-status language that Athletic Medicine, Athletic Performance, and coaches can all use without a fifteen-minute explanation.
75	
76	### 3. Knowledge-Behaviour Matrix (Webinar Parts II and III, Lab 1B, Student Workbook)
77	
78	What it is: a grid for auditing yourself and your staff on two independent axes. It evaluates capability and engagement, not personal worth.
79	
80	Knowledge axis (categories PDF-confirmed; the horizontal-axis placement comes from the webinar transcript only):
81	- Handbrake: does not understand the concepts or tech, may choose not to learn, increases everyone else's workload. Not automatically a bad person, but a bad fit if they stay stuck.
82	- Pawn: limited knowledge and experience but can execute clearly defined tasks and build momentum; with mentoring can grow into any piece on the board.
83	- Practitioner: solid professional, understands the space, competent with your technology, has frameworks and operates reliably. The backbone of the department.
84	- Operator: deep understanding plus broad experience; can design, integrate, and troubleshoot complex systems and see how technology, training, and operations connect.
85	
86	Behaviour axis (three levels PDF-confirmed; the vertical-axis placement comes from the webinar transcript only):
87	- Misaligned: does not buy the vision, does not care about direction, can actively undermine; eventually moved on or away from critical decisions.
88	- Coaster: happy to be here, does the minimum, useful in stable routine roles; you can carry one or two but cannot build a department from them.
89	- Catalyst: creates movement, influences others, does not always have the answer but finds the path; leaders with or without the title. Support, retain, give responsibility.
90	- (Webinar transcript adds a fourth top level, Beacon: knowledge plus passion to lead professionals across a domain. The PDFs and workbook stop at Catalyst.)
91	
92	How to run it with staff, following the Student Workbook (sections A to D):
93	1. A: each person writes their own definitions of the two axes and of all seven categories from memory, then checks against notes.
94	2. B1: self-place on each axis and write why.
95	3. B2: list two or three concrete behaviours as evidence for each self-rating.
96	4. B3: choose a three-to-five-year target on each axis and write what must change.
97	5. C1: map three to five people you work with above, beside, and below you, using initials or role titles only, with one example each.
98	6. C2: answer four tech and ops questions: who are the handbrakes with technology, who are the pawns with growth potential, who are the operators you can learn from, who behaves like a catalyst.
99	7. D1: three concrete actions in the next 30 to 90 days to move one step on either axis.
100	8. D2: pick one person from the table, name their current position and desired shift, and write specifically what you will do to help.
101	9. D3 (private): is anyone both handbrake and misaligned; what risk do they pose; what realistic options exist (role change, clearer expectations, eventual exit); what conversations have you been avoiding.
102	10. D4: complete "If I truly know myself and know my people, the one thing I must do differently over the next three months is..."
103	
104	Leader-side probes from Lab 1B: ask staff what they are working on for CPD, ask them to present ten minutes at a staff meeting on last month's work, and test technical understanding periodically. Use the matrix to design each person's CPD plan and to sanity-check hires.
105	
106	What it produces: a written map of the department, a personal development target, a CPD plan per person, and a list of the hard conversations.
107	
108	### 4. Tech Stack Reality Check (Lab 1C)
109	
110	What it is: a three-step audit that converts a pile of devices into a set of measurements you can trust.
111	
112	Step 1, inventory by measurement system (not brand):
113	- Your computer: what machine and specs, what software beyond spreadsheets, can you run data workflows, dashboards, or basic coding tools when needed.
114	- Wearables: GNSS plus IMU; know what is measured versus calculated and what assumptions sit under each output. Do not consume black-box metrics.
115	- Force plates: they measure force over time; understand impulse and time-specific strategies, not one jump-height number. Be able to explain the force-time curve.
116	- Force transducers and load cells: IMTP, iso squat and lunge, prone hamstring isometrics, eccentric hamstring tasks, dynamometry. A one-degree change in angle or alignment is a different test.
117	- Linear position transducers: standardise exercise naming, setup position, range-of-motion rules, valid-rep rules, and reporting rules (best rep versus average versus peak).
118	- Anything else you run (EMG etc.).
119	
120	Step 2, reliability: for each measurement, can you repeat the number within a small error band, within session and between sessions? Record where the evidence comes from: published data, internal repeat testing, or "we don't know yet".
121	
122	Step 3, procedures: draft a one-page procedure per tool covering warm-up, familiarisation, instructions, trial count, valid-rep and exclusion rules, reporting rule. Make it part of onboarding.
123	
124	What it produces: the five-item submission listed under Deliverables, and the department's procedural IP.
125	
126	### 5. Three failure modes, three disciplines, three rules (Podcast 1)
127	
128	Failure modes to watch for:
129	1. Protocol drift: same test name, different warm-up, angle, or execution; leaders who are not present must be able to trust the result.
130	2. Statistics-free interpretation: "he's improved, she's worse" with no grasp of change relative to device accuracy.
131	3. Communication chaos: dashboards exist but decisions are ad hoc, information is not aligned, actions are not assigned.
132	
133	Disciplines that close the gap:
134	1. Protocol: earn the right to compare. Lock down what the test is and what it is not, define valid reps and exclusions, standardise steps and instructions. Protects staff, supports onboarding, protects athletes from false conclusions.
135	2. Critical maths: every signal has information and noise. Establish system reliability (ICC, standard error of measurement, across different testers) and set thresholds for meaningful change. If you cannot explain why you trust the change, you cannot ask anyone to act on it.
136	3. Communication alignment: align language and procedures, and use consistent meeting structures that give the week a tempo and checkpoints tied to the competition cycle (whether a 14-day or 3-day lead-in).
137	
138	Closing rules: standardise data capture before scaling collection; define real change by understanding reliability in your environment; make decisions the product.
139	
140	### 6. Transcript-only concepts worth keeping
141	
142	- DIKW pyramid: data to information to knowledge to wisdom. Aim for the top of the pyramid in every report.
143	- Pick-up 52: the dashboard that drops all 52 cards and makes the coach sort them. Because you can build a visualisation does not mean you should.
144	- Rogers adoption curve: judge where a technology sits on it and where your people sit relative to it.
145	- Five things that will derail us: 60-second leadership quiz.
146	- Politician archetype: vocal on admin, silent on technical matters; test with a technical presentation.
147	
148	## Deliverables / exercises
149	
150	1. Common language document (Lab 1A): write down the shared vocabulary (means versus modality) and a program framework (CM² or your own), give every staff member a copy, and hold to it.
151	2. Five-things-that-will-derail-us list (Lab 1B Part 1, transcript-only): 60 seconds, write the five internal threats to the department.
152	3. Knowledge-Behaviour Profile Student Worksheet (Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook.pdf, five pages, sections A to D): definitions, self-audit with evidence, 3 to 5 year target, map of 3 to 5 people, tech and ops impact questions, 30 to 90 day personal actions, one person to develop, private hard-decision reflection, final sentence.
153	4. Tech Stack Reality Check submission (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.4):
154	   - List your tech stack grouped by measurement system, not brand.
155	   - For each tool, one line on what it truly measures (raw signal).
156	   - For each tool, one line on what you currently report (derived metrics).
157	   - For each tool, where reliability evidence comes from: published data, internal repeat testing, or "we don't know yet".
158	   - Pick one tool and draft a one-page procedure for it.
159	5. Implicit from the podcast: define, in writing, what real change means for each measurement in your environment before scaling collection.
160	
161	## Key quotes
162	
163	1. "Technology is there to measure and guide what matters. It doesn't decide what matters." (Lab_1A_Blog PDF p.2)
164	2. "You don't have to use those exact labels. But you do need something." (Lab_1A_Blog PDF p.3)
165	3. "No amount of software, dashboards or hardware will compensate for persistent handbrakes or misaligned staff." (Lab_1b_Blog PDF p.3)
166	4. "Many environments are tech-rich and procedure-poor." (Lab_1c PDF p.1)
167	5. "NordBord is a product. The test is eccentric knee flexor strength. If you confuse the two, you'll eventually confuse your results as well." (Lab_1c PDF p.1)
