# Module 1: People, Language, and Discipline Before Technology

Module 1 argues that the performance industry has spent the last fifteen years buying technology faster than it has built the people, shared language, and procedures needed to use it. Jason Weber (Old Bull Performance, creator of SpeedSig) traces the field from Milo of Croton to machine learning to show that the constraint is no longer access to information or equipment; it is vetting, filtering, and integrating what you already have. The module's fix has three layers: audit your people on a knowledge and behaviour matrix, agree a common language so cross-discipline staff can locate an athlete and a purpose in seconds, and inventory your tech stack by measurement system so you know what each device actually measures and whether you can repeat the number. The recurring principle is that discipline breeds freedom: standardised procedures produce reliability, reliability produces confidence, and confidence produces decisions you can defend. Every piece of equipment is a tool that must sit inside an operating system; the tool is not the upgrade, the discipline is.

## Lessons

### Webinar 1, Parts I to III: From Milo to Machine Learning (transcript-only, speaker unnamed but consistent with Weber)

- Part I is a history: Milo's calf as progressive overload; 1950s to 1970s birth of modern sport science (USSR institutes, Matveyev, Verkhoshansky); 1970s to 1990s institutes and specialisation; 1990s coach-sourced information (Poliquin, King, Chek) as a second stream beside academia; 2000 to 2020 the "technology quickening" of GPS/IMU, force plates, commercial biomechanics, and unfiltered social media.
- From 2020 the field is defined by scale and scrutiny rather than new science. By 2026 the constraint is not lack of information but vetting, filtering, and integrating it. AI is good for preliminary research and accelerating skilled coders, bad for oversimplification (staff handing in ChatGPT reviews instead of reading), and ugly when used to generate annual plans, rehab programs, or strength programs without the underlying skill.
- Part II: many current staff never studied the fundamentals and have never worked without GPS or force plates, so equipment is seen as environment rather than tool. Asked for a testing structure to integrate athletes, staff replied with a list of devices instead of the capacities they wanted to understand. Start with the question, not the equipment.
- A high-performance tech framework needs three things in staff: knowledge, curiosity, and work ethic. Rogers' adoption curve shows how technology moves through a population; higher knowledge and behaviour predicts earlier, more effective adoption (GPS was rejected by every code at a 1998 Australian meeting and is now universal).
- Part III applies the grid: a handbrake who is coasting is a red mark; a pawn who is a catalyst is worth investing in; an operator who is coasting may not help you build an elite team. Special Forces selection is cited: you want people who communicate and work in a team, not just the highest aptitude.
- The DIKW pyramid (data, information, knowledge, wisdom) frames the goal. "Pick-up 52" dashboards make the coach or medical colleague do the interpretation. Start with the recipient's question, define equipment and standards, assess from multiple perspectives (one favourable eccentric hamstring number does not equal readiness), and simplify carefully (SpeedSig's classification of 64 back-end data points into one athlete type is his product example).

### Lab 1A: Building a Common Language (transcript plus Lab_1A_Blog PDF)

- Everyone speaks English but not the same language. Staff from different disciplines bring different histories and mentors; without a shared framework meetings degrade into arguments about exercises instead of solutions for athletes.
- Means versus modality (from old Russian training literature): means is why, modality is what. An A-skip is one modality that can serve as a warm-up means or a low-level plyometric means. Agree the means, then be flexible on modality.
- Technology comes third, not first: means, then modality, then technology.
- CM² (Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum) is a shared athlete map so anyone can answer "where does this athlete currently live in our model" in one sentence.
- You do not have to use these labels, but you must have something: written down, distributed, and stuck to.

### Lab 1B, Parts 1 and 2: People and Effective Ops (transcripts plus Lab_1b_Blog PDF and Student Workbook)

- Sun Tzu's "know thyself and know thy enemy" reframed: the enemy is internal constraints, people who quietly slow things down, knowledge gaps nobody admits, behaviours that do not match the standards on the wall.
- First question for any leader: what could derail this? A 60-second exercise: write down the five things that will stop this department from working.
- Leadership is not a badge; aspiring leaders must practice reading themselves and their environment before they get the title.
- The knowledge and behaviour axes combine into an ops audit that drives decisions on mentoring, responsibility, and who should not be in the system. Mentors must have worked at the level you aspire to.
- Practical tests of where people sit: ask about CPD, have them present ten minutes at a staff meeting on last month's work, put them on the spot on technical matters. Transcript-only "politician" archetype: vocal on admin and allowances, silent on technical matters.
- The matrix is a CPD design tool for leaders and an honest self-check for staff, ideally cross-checked with your boss. Misaligned people need to be managed out or away from critical decisions.

### Lab 1C: The Tech Stack Audit (transcript plus Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit PDF; the Free Version is byte-identical)

- Most environments are tech-rich and procedure-poor. The industry confuses brands with tests ("we're doing NordBord" names a product; the test is eccentric knee flexor strength).
- Step one is an inventory by measurement system, starting with the most overlooked tool: your computer, which most practitioners use like a typewriter.
- Step two is reliability: can you repeat the number within a small error band, within and between sessions? In-house reliability matters more than published because your staff, setup, and athletes create your real-world error.
- Step three is procedures: the hidden multiplier and your professional IP, locked and part of onboarding. A leader should be able to walk into any environment and say "these are our procedures, this is our starting point."
- Discipline breeds freedom (Willink). Do not buy new tech; order the tech you have and earn the right to trust it.

### Podcast 1: The False Promise of Technology without Discipline (transcript plus False_Promise blog PDF; Free Version byte-identical)

- Tools do not create clarity; discipline does. Without discipline more data means more noise, more arguments, and less trust.
- Discipline means repeatable behaviour: standardised protocols, correct maths and statistics, consistent operations. Missing any one turns the tool into a random number generator.
- Three failure modes, three disciplines, three closing rules (detailed under Frameworks).
- False promise sounds like: "we bought the system so now we have objective truth", "the dashboard says red so we pulled him", "we monitor everything all the time".

## Frameworks and tools taught

### 1. Means versus Modality, then Technology (Lab 1A)

What it is: a two-word vocabulary that separates purpose from activity, plus a fixed ordering that puts equipment last.

How to run it:
1. For any drill, exercise, or test in a program, ask "what's the means?" (what physical quality or adaptation are we trying to change: strength, stiffness, deceleration, asymmetry, rehab tolerance).
2. Only then discuss the modality (the specific drill, lift, or test) and accept that the same modality can serve different means.
3. Only then ask what technology can evaluate or support that work.
4. In staff meetings, ban "why are you using that drill" and "I don't like that exercise"; replace with "what are you trying to achieve with that drill?"

What it produces: shorter meetings, exercise selection defended by intent, and a habit of choosing tests by question rather than by available kit.

### 2. CM² athlete map: Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum (Lab 1A)

What it is: a four-stage progression model that gives every discipline one sentence to locate an athlete.

Stages:
1. Control: single joints or very simple patterns; regain or establish basic control; early rehab or very low training age. Move through it as fast as possible; do not park athletes in isolated clams and wall balances once they have the basics.
2. Movement: link joints into coordinated, repeatable multi-joint patterns; move viably as a whole system without falling apart.
3. Capacity: volume, tolerance, robustness; build the engine to handle training and competition loads; developing athletes live here for large parts of the year.
4. Maximum: highest intensities (max strength, power, speed); short exposures balanced against capacity; you oscillate between capacity and maximum rather than living in maximum.

How to run it: agree the stage definitions in writing, give every staff member a copy, and use the phrases in every athlete conversation ("she's in a movement-capacity block", "he's not moving well, pull him back to control", "we can't justify maximum work until his capacity improves"). Adapt the labels if you like but keep one shared map.

What it produces: a common athlete-status language that Athletic Medicine, Athletic Performance, and coaches can all use without a fifteen-minute explanation.

### 3. Knowledge-Behaviour Matrix (Webinar Parts II and III, Lab 1B, Student Workbook)

What it is: a grid for auditing yourself and your staff on two independent axes. It evaluates capability and engagement, not personal worth.

Knowledge axis (categories PDF-confirmed; the horizontal-axis placement comes from the webinar transcript only):
- Handbrake: does not understand the concepts or tech, may choose not to learn, increases everyone else's workload. Not automatically a bad person, but a bad fit if they stay stuck.
- Pawn: limited knowledge and experience but can execute clearly defined tasks and build momentum; with mentoring can grow into any piece on the board.
- Practitioner: solid professional, understands the space, competent with your technology, has frameworks and operates reliably. The backbone of the department.
- Operator: deep understanding plus broad experience; can design, integrate, and troubleshoot complex systems and see how technology, training, and operations connect.

Behaviour axis (three levels PDF-confirmed; the vertical-axis placement comes from the webinar transcript only):
- Misaligned: does not buy the vision, does not care about direction, can actively undermine; eventually moved on or away from critical decisions.
- Coaster: happy to be here, does the minimum, useful in stable routine roles; you can carry one or two but cannot build a department from them.
- Catalyst: creates movement, influences others, does not always have the answer but finds the path; leaders with or without the title. Support, retain, give responsibility.
- (Webinar transcript adds a fourth top level, Beacon: knowledge plus passion to lead professionals across a domain. The PDFs and workbook stop at Catalyst.)

How to run it with staff, following the Student Workbook (sections A to D):
1. A: each person writes their own definitions of the two axes and of all seven categories from memory, then checks against notes.
2. B1: self-place on each axis and write why.
3. B2: list two or three concrete behaviours as evidence for each self-rating.
4. B3: choose a three-to-five-year target on each axis and write what must change.
5. C1: map three to five people you work with above, beside, and below you, using initials or role titles only, with one example each.
6. C2: answer four tech and ops questions: who are the handbrakes with technology, who are the pawns with growth potential, who are the operators you can learn from, who behaves like a catalyst.
7. D1: three concrete actions in the next 30 to 90 days to move one step on either axis.
8. D2: pick one person from the table, name their current position and desired shift, and write specifically what you will do to help.
9. D3 (private): is anyone both handbrake and misaligned; what risk do they pose; what realistic options exist (role change, clearer expectations, eventual exit); what conversations have you been avoiding.
10. D4: complete "If I truly know myself and know my people, the one thing I must do differently over the next three months is..."

Leader-side probes from Lab 1B: ask staff what they are working on for CPD, ask them to present ten minutes at a staff meeting on last month's work, and test technical understanding periodically. Use the matrix to design each person's CPD plan and to sanity-check hires.

What it produces: a written map of the department, a personal development target, a CPD plan per person, and a list of the hard conversations.

### 4. Tech Stack Reality Check (Lab 1C)

What it is: a three-step audit that converts a pile of devices into a set of measurements you can trust.

Step 1, inventory by measurement system (not brand):
- Your computer: what machine and specs, what software beyond spreadsheets, can you run data workflows, dashboards, or basic coding tools when needed.
- Wearables: GNSS plus IMU; know what is measured versus calculated and what assumptions sit under each output. Do not consume black-box metrics.
- Force plates: they measure force over time; understand impulse and time-specific strategies, not one jump-height number. Be able to explain the force-time curve.
- Force transducers and load cells: IMTP, iso squat and lunge, prone hamstring isometrics, eccentric hamstring tasks, dynamometry. A one-degree change in angle or alignment is a different test.
- Linear position transducers: standardise exercise naming, setup position, range-of-motion rules, valid-rep rules, and reporting rules (best rep versus average versus peak).
- Anything else you run (EMG etc.).

Step 2, reliability: for each measurement, can you repeat the number within a small error band, within session and between sessions? Record where the evidence comes from: published data, internal repeat testing, or "we don't know yet".

Step 3, procedures: draft a one-page procedure per tool covering warm-up, familiarisation, instructions, trial count, valid-rep and exclusion rules, reporting rule. Make it part of onboarding.

What it produces: the five-item submission listed under Deliverables, and the department's procedural IP.

### 5. Three failure modes, three disciplines, three rules (Podcast 1)

Failure modes to watch for:
1. Protocol drift: same test name, different warm-up, angle, or execution; leaders who are not present must be able to trust the result.
2. Statistics-free interpretation: "he's improved, she's worse" with no grasp of change relative to device accuracy.
3. Communication chaos: dashboards exist but decisions are ad hoc, information is not aligned, actions are not assigned.

Disciplines that close the gap:
1. Protocol: earn the right to compare. Lock down what the test is and what it is not, define valid reps and exclusions, standardise steps and instructions. Protects staff, supports onboarding, protects athletes from false conclusions.
2. Critical maths: every signal has information and noise. Establish system reliability (ICC, standard error of measurement, across different testers) and set thresholds for meaningful change. If you cannot explain why you trust the change, you cannot ask anyone to act on it.
3. Communication alignment: align language and procedures, and use consistent meeting structures that give the week a tempo and checkpoints tied to the competition cycle (whether a 14-day or 3-day lead-in).

Closing rules: standardise data capture before scaling collection; define real change by understanding reliability in your environment; make decisions the product.

### 6. Transcript-only concepts worth keeping

- DIKW pyramid: data to information to knowledge to wisdom. Aim for the top of the pyramid in every report.
- Pick-up 52: the dashboard that drops all 52 cards and makes the coach sort them. Because you can build a visualisation does not mean you should.
- Rogers adoption curve: judge where a technology sits on it and where your people sit relative to it.
- Five things that will derail us: 60-second leadership quiz.
- Politician archetype: vocal on admin, silent on technical matters; test with a technical presentation.

## Deliverables / exercises

1. Common language document (Lab 1A): write down the shared vocabulary (means versus modality) and a program framework (CM² or your own), give every staff member a copy, and hold to it.
2. Five-things-that-will-derail-us list (Lab 1B Part 1, transcript-only): 60 seconds, write the five internal threats to the department.
3. Knowledge-Behaviour Profile Student Worksheet (Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook.pdf, five pages, sections A to D): definitions, self-audit with evidence, 3 to 5 year target, map of 3 to 5 people, tech and ops impact questions, 30 to 90 day personal actions, one person to develop, private hard-decision reflection, final sentence.
4. Tech Stack Reality Check submission (Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit.pdf p.4):
   - List your tech stack grouped by measurement system, not brand.
   - For each tool, one line on what it truly measures (raw signal).
   - For each tool, one line on what you currently report (derived metrics).
   - For each tool, where reliability evidence comes from: published data, internal repeat testing, or "we don't know yet".
   - Pick one tool and draft a one-page procedure for it.
5. Implicit from the podcast: define, in writing, what real change means for each measurement in your environment before scaling collection.

## Key quotes

1. "Technology is there to measure and guide what matters. It doesn't decide what matters." (Lab_1A_Blog PDF p.2)
2. "You don't have to use those exact labels. But you do need something." (Lab_1A_Blog PDF p.3)
3. "No amount of software, dashboards or hardware will compensate for persistent handbrakes or misaligned staff." (Lab_1b_Blog PDF p.3)
4. "Many environments are tech-rich and procedure-poor." (Lab_1c PDF p.1)
5. "NordBord is a product. The test is eccentric knee flexor strength. If you confuse the two, you'll eventually confuse your results as well." (Lab_1c PDF p.1)
6. "If your setup changes, your test changes." (Lab_1c PDF p.2)
7. "You'll chase noise and call it insight." (Lab_1c PDF p.3)
8. "The device doesn't create trust. Your procedure does." (Lab_1c PDF p.3)
9. "Earn the right to compare. If you can't repeat it, you can't learn from it." (False_Promise PDF p.1; Podcast 1 approx 04:24)
10. "The tool is not the upgrade, discipline is." (False_Promise PDF p.2, punctuation adjusted; Podcast 1 approx 09:36)

1	# Module 2: Turning Technology Into Defensible Decisions
2	
3	Module 2 argues that technology is an accelerator of good practice, not a source of it, and that a department only gets value from its tools when each one sits inside a designed workflow that ends in a decision. The five labs build a single chain: separate what a tool measures from what staff infer (2A), map every technology to the question it answers and the people who own each step (2B), decide in advance whether a metric is being monitored for short-term status or tested for long-term progress (2C), pre-agree the checkpoints where results become go, modify, or stop calls (2D), and quantify measurement noise so those checkpoints hold up under pressure (2E). Podcast 2 and its companion blog close the module with two case studies showing that no single signal, whether a scary video clip or a scan, should decide an outcome; the right question is "do we have sufficient information to act?" The module's consistent leadership message is that structure set up before pressure arrives is what protects staff, coaches, and athletes from emotional single-signal reactions.
4	
5	## Lessons
6	
7	### Lab 2A: Measurement vs Inference (video 6:17; PDF "What Is the Role of Technology?", 4 pp.)
8	
9	- Technology became "furniture" for anyone who entered high-performance sport after about 2010; because it is normal, people stop thinking about what it actually does and start over-claiming what it can tell them (PDF p.1).
10	- Core principle: "Technology accelerates practice. It does not create practice." The foundation is still biology, adaptation, progressive load, recovery, and time (PDF p.1). The video attributes the accelerator idea to Jim Collins's Good to Great (transcript ~00:39).
11	- Measurement is what the tool directly captures: force over time (force plates), distance and speed estimates (GNSS/GPS), displacement and velocity (linear transducers), task outcomes such as jump height or sprint time. Inference is what staff think it implies: tissue stress, readiness, "neural fatigue," "healed tissue," injury risk (PDF pp.1-2).
12	- A force plate can say a jump changed; it cannot say the central nervous system is compromised. GPS can say external work changed; it cannot say what stress the tissue experienced (PDF p.2).
13	- Humans are redundant systems. The same output can hide a different strategy, so the question is never only "did they hit the number?" but "how did they hit the number, and what happens when we expose them again?" (PDF p.2).
14	- Matching a previous NordBord score is a valuable data point, not a clearance decision by itself (PDF p.3). The fix is triangulation plus probabilistic language.
15	
16	### Lab 2B: Capability and Workflow Audit (video 4:35; PDF 3 pp.)
17	
18	- Small environments align naturally because everyone talks daily. As staff, tools, and handoffs grow, "alignment must be designed, not hoped for" (PDF p.1).
19	- Capability audit is "tool truth": what it measures, what it does not measure, where its output turns into inference. Workflow audit is where most departments fail: who captures, how it is processed (vendor, in-house code, SpeedSig, dashboards), who interprets, how it is communicated, where the decision gets made (PDF p.1).
20	- Strategy is the highway (direction, standards, key questions). Tactics are lane changes (which tool, how to adjust tests, timing, exposure). The goal is tactical freedom inside strategic alignment; the video calls this leading by strategic intent and links it to special forces leadership (PDF pp.1-2; transcript ~01:08).
21	- The payoff is a leadership asset: clarity and onboarding for staff, discipline for the department, a clean budget argument for what is missing, and documented procedures for performance review (PDF p.3).
22	- The matrix is repeatable and travels with you across clubs; technologies change over time but not overnight (PDF p.3).
23	
24	### Lab 2C: Monitoring vs Testing (video 8:13; full and Free Version are byte-identical; PDF 3 pp.)
25	
26	- Monitoring is short-term (days to weeks) and asks "has something changed right now?" It informs load adjustments, recovery, exposure progression or regression, and short-term risk. "Monitoring is status and trend" (PDF p.1).
27	- Testing is longer reach (weeks to months) and asks "have we improved capacity across a training phase?" Pre-season start vs end, block one vs block two, year one vs year five. "Testing is progress" (PDF p.1).
28	- Do not misuse methods. Rolling averages and exponentially weighted moving averages are good at "is the athlete drifting from baseline this week?" but not at phase-to-phase change; because the reference moves with the data, a slow decay never falls outside the bounds of normal (PDF pp.1-2; transcript ~02:13). Long-term change needs pre vs post or block vs block comparisons; the video mentions something as simple as an ANOVA (transcript ~02:56).
29	- The procedure rule: start with the quality you want to evaluate, decide whether you are monitoring or testing, then choose the technology, then assign it to a schedule. "We have force plates, so we should jump" is technology-led practice and creates noise (PDF p.2).
30	- Communicate to coaches before pressure arrives using five questions: what are we evaluating, why, how often, what output will you receive, what will we do if it changes. "For this time commitment, here's what you get back" (PDF p.2). The video adds a margin-of-error example from AFL time trials: a two-second miss inside known reliable-change error does not trigger extra training (transcript ~06:04).
31	- For aspiring leaders, the video says this belongs in a "first 90 plan" for a new role (transcript ~04:48). It also references the data, information, knowledge, wisdom ladder as the paradigm for what gets pushed up to coaches (transcript ~05:22).
32	
33	### Lab 2D: Decision Gates (video 4:46; PDF "Designing Decision Gates", 3 pp.)
34	
35	- A decision gate is a predefined checkpoint in a workflow where agreed criteria are reviewed and a clear call is made before progressing: Go / Modify / Stop. Gates stop departments from "dumping data" on coaches and senior medical staff and hoping everyone interprets it the same way (PDF p.1).
36	- Decision gates already exist in everything a department does; the point is to design and control them so they create clarity instead of random data followed by a random response (transcript ~00:49).
37	- The most common failure is vagueness. "Hamstring injury" or "hamstring capacity" is not a gate; "eccentric knee flexor strength" or "sprint exposure tolerance at a defined speed band and volume" is (PDF p.1).
38	- Rules agreed before the pressure arrives reduce debate, especially around selection, when emotion enters the room (PDF p.2; transcript ~03:04).
39	- Timeframes are part of the gate. Different sports have different realities: an NFL-scale organisation may get imaging straight off the field; a lower-funded program may wait days. Set expectations early so timelines are not improvised after an injury (PDF p.2; transcript ~03:29).
40	- The video's framing: a gate is not just a number, it is a pathway with temporal control; "discipline equals freedom" (transcript ~04:09).
41	
42	### Lab 2E: The Critical Math That Cannot Be Ignored (video 5:16; PDF 3 pp.)
43	
44	- Technology provides measurement; the system provides interpretation. The one question technology has to answer with confidence is "is this change real, or is it noise?" Without the math you can collect data but cannot interpret it responsibly or build gates that hold under pressure (PDF p.1).
45	- Two paths: system-level reliability (can we trust the test at all?) and individual-level monitoring sensitivity (can we detect meaningful change in this athlete?) (PDF p.1).
46	- Reliability is the whole system, not the device: equipment, protocol, tester, environment, and the athlete's execution (PDF p.1).
47	- MDC answers "is it beyond noise?" SWC answers "is it worth caring about?" Both matter and serve different purposes (PDF p.1).
48	- Rate of force development is the classic noisy metric because execution consistency, onset detection choices, and small timing differences all move the number. When a metric is noisy: widen thresholds, tighten the protocol, or choose a more stable metric for gates (PDF p.2). The video's anecdote is a physio arriving with "RFD is off by 12%" when 12% sits well inside the MDC (transcript ~04:13).
49	- Leadership angle: if staff use tests with unknown reliability, there is no foundation for trust in any number they bring you. Rigour gives credibility, consistent reporting, defensible thresholds, and gates that work (PDF p.2).
50	
51	### Podcast 2: Evidence Stacking (audio 18:21; PDF "Do We Have Sufficient Information to Act?", SpeedSig/OBP companion blog, 4 pp.)
52	
53	- Reframes the series question from "how much is enough to act?" to "do we have sufficient information to act?" The most dangerous decisions in high performance are the fastest ones (PDF p.1).
54	- A signal can be anything: a mechanism on video, a player's reaction, a clinical test, a scan, a hop distance, a single device metric, a coach's comment, or the club's own recent injury history. The mistake is treating any one of them as the verdict (PDF p.1).
55	- Case 1: a professional soccer forward with bilateral ACL history has an ugly valgus mechanism on video, plays the second half, gets called "out, ACL" by staff primed by recent ACL injuries at the club, then stacks MRI with no reported ACL damage, a full hop within about 12 hours, a known 6.2 m three-hop baseline repeated four times, agility passes, and training at pace. He failed one of six checks and progressed (PDF pp.1-3).
56	- Case 2: an AFL hamstring three weeks before finals, doctors say "no chance," the high performance manager says "stop, one step at a time," next-day walking and range of motion are good, radiology is inconclusive, and a pre-injury SpeedSig running profile lets them confirm at 5.5 m/s that he is running the same way as before injury. He returned and did not miss another game until the team exited finals (PDF p.3); the podcast adds, hedged with "I think," that he missed the first final (transcript ~17:04).
57	- Lesson from case 2: the gap is often gym testing to field performance, and generic GPS alone will not answer the "how" question (PDF p.3).
58	- Leadership: coaches want certainty, staff feel pressure, doctors and physios are human, recent injuries distort judgement, a run of similar injuries can create a false sense of a trend. In unstable environments (new staff, preseason in a week) the leader may need to say "this is how we will proceed; we'll refine it together" (PDF p.3).

60	## Frameworks and tools taught
61	
62	### 1. Measurement, Inference, Probability, Next Step (Lab 2A)
63	
64	What it is: a four-part communication structure that replaces absolutes ("he's ready," "this shows neural fatigue") with labelled inference.
65	
66	How to run it (PDF pp.3-4):
67	1. What we measured (facts). Name the tests and the direction of each result.
68	2. What it suggests (inference). Label it as inference.
69	3. How confident we are (probability). Say whether probability is improving, stable, or falling.
70	4. What we recommend next (progression or exposure plan).
71	
72	Worked example from the PDF (p.4): "We measured five markers associated with hamstring function and running exposure. All are stable pre-to-post and again at 24 hours. Probability is improving that he is ready for the next level of exposure. Next step: controlled progression toward match demands."
73	
74	The video's one-line axiom (transcript ~05:50): report what you measure, state what you infer, assign a probability, then recommend the next exposure.
75	
76	What it produces: a coach-facing statement that cannot be accused of over-claiming what the tool knows.
77	
78	### 2. Triangulation plan (Lab 2A)
79	
80	What it is: building a case for readiness from multiple angles instead of one test returning to baseline.
81	
82	Hamstring return-to-play example (PDF p.3): eccentric knee flexor strength; isometric posterior-chain strength; running exposure up to meaningful speed; movement mechanics checks where available; post-exposure response immediately and at 24 hours. The video adds isometrics at inner and outer range and at the hip, jump and hop tests on a force plate for stretch-shortening cycle, and a running mechanics profile to confirm the athlete is achieving speed in an expected way (transcript ~04:13).
83	
84	Rule: if all tests are positive, exposures are tolerated, and performance holds after load, then the probability improves that the athlete is ready to progress. Probability improves is not certainty (PDF p.3).
85	
86	What it produces: a 4-6 data-point plan per injury type with a built-in post-exposure check.
87	
88	### 3. Capability and Workflow Matrix (Lab 2B)
89	
90	What it is: a one-page grid that maps every technology to the questions it answers and the workflow that carries its output to a decision.
91	
92	How to build it (PDF p.2):
93	1. Rows = technologies. List everything: computer and software stack, GPS/IMU, force plates, load cells and force transducers, linear transducers, video tools, wellness and subjective measures.
94	2. Columns = applications. Option A by domain (rehab, performance, return-to-play, monitoring). Option B by question (hamstring injury, calf injury, adductor/groin, speed development, maximum strength, deceleration ability, fatigue monitoring).
95	3. Fill each cell with four items: Purpose (what question it answers), Output (the metric or report delivered), Owner (who is responsible), Workflow (capture, process, interpret, communicate, decision).
96	
97	The video splits Owner further: who owns the capture, who owns the understanding and determines reliability, who maintains the upkeep (transcript ~02:31).
98	
99	Worked cells (PDF pp.2-3):
100	- Hamstring rehab (triangulation workflow): force transducer or dynamometry gives a strength capacity trend; GPS/IMU gives exposure dose (high-speed work, accelerations); mechanics check gives strategy change vs baseline; response checks give immediate and 24-hour stability. Workflow names who runs the test, where the data lives, who processes it, how it is reported, who makes the progression decision. The video's version: physio owns capture, sports science owns the reporting template (transcript ~02:59).
101	- Deceleration capacity (performance workflow): GPS/IMU captures high-intensity deceleration events; data may need processing in Python, R, or SpeedSig; output is a trend report plus exposure tolerance summary; decision is programming adjustment (load, density, drill selection).
102	
103	What it produces: a matrix, plus a list of gaps (questions you cannot currently answer), bottlenecks (where workflow breaks), and handoff risks (where communication fails). The video's closing test, as best the transcript can be read: if it is not in the matrix it is not in the workflow, and if it is not in the workflow it does not exist (transcript ~04:12, wording garbled).
104	
105	### 4. Monitoring vs Testing procedure rule (Lab 2C)
106	
107	What it is: an ordering rule that prevents technology-led practice.
108	
109	Steps (PDF p.2; transcript ~03:32):
110	1. Start with the quality you want to evaluate (what capacity matters for this sport, coach, phase, athlete).
111	2. Decide whether you are monitoring it (short-term status, days to weeks) or testing it (phase change, weeks to months), or both at different times.
112	3. Choose the technology.
113	4. Assign it to a schedule inside the periodised plan. Do not make it random. Injury programs should state in advance when testing happens, with flexibility for acute availability questions.
114	5. Match the analysis to the horizon: rolling averages and EWMA for short-term drift; pre vs post or block vs block comparisons for phase change.
115	
116	What it produces: definitions of monitoring and testing, and for each key quality a stated horizon, frequency, and output.
117	
118	### 5. Coach communication script (Lab 2C)
119	
120	What it is: a five-question brief to run with a new coach or staff group before data collection starts (PDF p.2).
121	
122	- What are we evaluating?
123	- Why are we evaluating it?
124	- How often will we do it?
125	- What will you receive as output?
126	- What will we do if it changes?
127	
128	The video's script form (transcript ~05:31): "We're evaluating X because of Y. We'll do it this often. This is when the test will occur. I'll get the information to you in this period. If we get this result, this is what we're going to do." Include margin of error so a small miss is not treated as meaningful.
129	
130	What it produces: coach expectations set before a surprise result creates pressure.
131	
132	### 6. Decision matrix (Lab 2C)
133	
134	What it is: the bridge from a result to an action. Format (PDF p.2): if we get this result, we do these steps, owned by these people, reviewed at this time point.
135	
136	Hamstring example (PDF p.2): if eccentric knee flexor force drops meaningfully, confirm test quality and re-test; physio screen plus range-of-motion checks as indicated; adjust exposure plan; reassess response immediately and at 24 hours; progress only when stable. The video's version assigns owners (S&C and sports science confirm the test; physio does clinical strain, ROM, palpation; the S&C coach adjusts the exposure plan for 48 to 72 hours; recheck within 24 hours) (transcript ~07:00). The two versions differ slightly on timing; treat them as illustrative, not as a protocol.
137	
138	What it produces: for one quality, an "if improves" action, an "if declines" action, owners for each step, and a re-check time.
139	
140	### 7. Five-part Decision Gate (Lab 2D)
141	
142	What it is: a predefined checkpoint with agreed criteria and a forced decision (Go / Modify / Stop).
143	
144	The five parts (PDF pp.1-2):
145	1. What is being evaluated. Name the capacity and the contraction or task precisely: eccentric knee flexor strength, isometric hip extension strength, sprint exposure tolerance (defined speed band and volume), deceleration exposure tolerance (defined intensity and count).
146	2. Criteria. Pass (green): proceed. Fail (red): stop or regress. Borderline (amber): confirm, repeat, or add another data point. Also define what counts as a breach so people do not argue afterwards. The video adds that criteria must be statistically grounded: different to this person, to their history, and to the population (transcript ~01:46).
147	3. Decision options. Progress, Hold, Regress, Refer (to medical lead), Escalate (specialist imaging or surgical opinion). Options should reflect the sport and medical setup.
148	4. Ownership. Who provides inputs, who interprets results, who owns the final call. Performance and medical staff often share inputs but one role owns the decision, especially in return-to-play progression.
149	5. Next step. Every gate triggers immediate action with a time window. PDF examples: pass, progress to next exposure stage; fail, regress and re-test in 72 hours; borderline, repeat test plus add another measure and set the review time.
150	
151	Timeframes are built in (PDF p.2): "First clinical review happens within X hours. Imaging is expected within Y days if criteria are met. First progression gate occurs on Day Z, assuming symptoms and function allow."
152	
153	What it produces: two written gates (one performance, one rehab) each with all five parts.
154	
155	### 8. Reliability and threshold concepts (Lab 2E)
156	
157	What it is: the minimum statistical vocabulary underneath every gate. The course teaches definitions and a decision rule; it does not present computational formulas.
158	
159	Path 1, system-level reliability (PDF p.1):
160	- ICC (intraclass correlation coefficient): how consistently athletes are ranked across repeated trials. Relative reliability.
161	- SEM / TE (standard error of measurement / typical error): the size of the noise in the units you care about. Absolute reliability. "SEM/TE tells you how noisy the test is."
162	- MDC95 (minimal detectable change at 95% confidence): how much change is required to be confident the shift is beyond typical measurement noise. "MDC95 tells you how much change you need before you can call it real."
163	
164	Path 2, individual-level monitoring sensitivity (PDF p.1):
165	- Typical error / within-athlete variability, often summarised as CV% for repeated measures.
166	- SWC (smallest worthwhile change): the smallest change that is practically meaningful, not just statistically real.
167	
168	Decision logic (PDF p.2; transcript ~03:34):
169	- Change below MDC95: likely noise.
170	- Change above MDC95: likely real.
171	- Change above SWC: likely meaningful.
172	- Change above both: act with confidence.
173	- Change real but not meaningful: note it, watch it, do not overreact.
174	- Neither: treat any difference as noise.
175	
176	Noisy metric rule (PDF p.2): widen thresholds, tighten the protocol, or choose a more stable metric for gates. RFD is the named example.
177	
178	Note for staff use: the standard computational formulas for SEM, MDC95, and SWC are not given in the course materials; the lab expects the department to already have or compute these values for its own tests.
179	
180	### 9. CM² progression: Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum (Podcast 2)
181	
182	What it is: a defensible step-by-step rehab progression. Start at the base and earn the next step (PDF p.2; transcript ~09:54).
183	
184	1. Control: single-joint control, range of motion, joint tolerance (effusion, pain behaviour).
185	2. Movement: sequencing hip, knee, and ankle together; simple patterns before complex.
186	3. Capacity: clearance tests appropriate to the injury; hops, deceleration, strength outputs.
187	4. Maximum / Performance: sport-specific exposures; fatigue-resilient execution at relevant pace.
188	
189	### 10. Six-check Evidence Stack (Podcast 2)
190	
191	What it is: a checklist to remove emotion and stop a department reacting to one dramatic input. Rule: no single signal decides the outcome (PDF pp.2-4; transcript ~10:45).
192	
193	1. Mechanism: was there a plausible mechanism, and what does video actually show and not show (load, weight-bearing)?
194	2. Radiology: use it but it is interpretive; clear structural disruption is clear, tissue "signal" needs context.
195	3. Clinical exam: range of motion, effusion, functional limp, key ligament tests (anterior drawer endpoint), gait.
196	4. Fundamental control and movement checks: can they control the joint, can they sequence cleanly?
197	5. Capacity tests (clearance tests): hops, deceleration, strength and SSC outputs relevant to the tissue and sport.
198	6. Performance-relevant functional tests: on-field movement, agility and exposure at pace, execution without breakdown under fatigue.
199	
200	Count passes against fails. In the soccer case the athlete failed one of six and passed the rest, which shifted the decision from fear to probability.
201	
202	### 11. Statistics-to-decision sequence (Podcast 2 blog)
203	
204	Five steps (PDF p.3): test your tests (system reliability); build athlete baselines early; define thresholds (normal variation, SWC, what counts as meaningful in your world); use multiple signals; bridge data to decisions so you can say "this is what we saw, this is what it means, this is what we do next." The goal is not perfect certainty but reducing avoidable error.

294	## Applicability notes
295	
296	- The Capability and Workflow Matrix maps directly onto the Applied Performance stack. Rows: Catapult GPS, VALD force plates, VALD dynamometry (NordBord, ForceFrame, DynaMo), the AMS, video, wellness. Columns by question the football and Olympic sport coaches actually ask. The matrix exposes the cells where the AMS holds data nobody acts on, and the cells where Athletic Performance captures a metric but Athletic Medicine never sees it. It also doubles as the onboarding document for new Athletic Performance staff and the budget justification for the next VALD or Catapult renewal.
297	- Lab 2A's NordBord example is a direct warning for VALD reporting: a returning athlete matching their pre-injury eccentric knee flexor score is one data point in a triangulation, not a return-to-play clearance. Athletic Performance and Athletic Medicine should agree that the AMS return-to-play summary reports the measured markers, the inference, the confidence, and the next exposure step rather than a "cleared / not cleared" flag.
298	- Lab 2C forces a decision about which Catapult and VALD outputs are monitoring and which are testing. Daily CMJ on force plates and session high-speed running from Catapult are monitoring (EWMA and rolling baselines in the AMS are appropriate). Pre-camp vs post-camp or block-to-block strength and jump batteries are testing and need pre vs post comparison, not the AMS's continuous smoothing. Coaches should be told which is which before the season starts, using the five-question script.
299	- Lab 2E is the technical work the department owes itself. Every VALD and Catapult metric used in a decision gate needs its own ICC, SEM/TE, and MDC95 from Baylor's own equipment, protocol, testers, and environment, plus a within-athlete CV% and SWC for the monitored metrics. Vendor-published reliability is a starting point, not a substitute. Force plate RFD and other early-phase force-time metrics should be treated as noisy until proven otherwise; use wider bands or a more stable metric for gates.
300	- Decision gates and the decision matrix belong in the AMS as written rules with owners: what quality, what threshold in local MDC and SWC units, what options, who in Athletic Medicine owns the return-to-play call and who in Athletic Performance owns the exposure adjustment, and the re-check window. Writing timeframes into the gate (first clinical review within X hours, imaging within Y days, first progression gate on Day Z) is what stops a head coach's Sunday phone call from setting the timeline.
301	- The six-check evidence stack is a shared language for Athletic Performance and Athletic Medicine case reviews after an in-game incident. Mechanism from film, radiology, clinical exam, control and movement, capacity tests on VALD, and performance-relevant field exposure on Catapult give both groups a structured way to say "we have five of six" instead of reacting to the clip. The AFL case shows why a pre-injury running profile from GPS matters: the return-to-run question is not only "can he hit 5.5 m/s" but "is he running the same way he did before."

# Module 2: Turning Technology Into Defensible Decisions

Module 2 argues that technology is an accelerator of good practice, not a source of it, and that a department only gets value from its tools when each one sits inside a designed workflow that ends in a decision. The five labs build a single chain: separate what a tool measures from what staff infer (2A), map every technology to the question it answers and the people who own each step (2B), decide in advance whether a metric is being monitored for short-term status or tested for long-term progress (2C), pre-agree the checkpoints where results become go, modify, or stop calls (2D), and quantify measurement noise so those checkpoints hold up under pressure (2E). Podcast 2 and its companion blog close the module with two case studies showing that no single signal, whether a scary video clip or a scan, should decide an outcome; the right question is "do we have sufficient information to act?" The module's consistent leadership message is that structure set up before pressure arrives is what protects staff, coaches, and athletes from emotional single-signal reactions.

## Lessons

### Lab 2A: Measurement vs Inference (video 6:17; PDF "What Is the Role of Technology?", 4 pp.)

- Technology became "furniture" for anyone who entered high-performance sport after about 2010; because it is normal, people stop thinking about what it actually does and start over-claiming what it can tell them (PDF p.1).
- Core principle: "Technology accelerates practice. It does not create practice." The foundation is still biology, adaptation, progressive load, recovery, and time (PDF p.1). The video attributes the accelerator idea to Jim Collins's Good to Great (transcript ~00:39).
- Measurement is what the tool directly captures: force over time (force plates), distance and speed estimates (GNSS/GPS), displacement and velocity (linear transducers), task outcomes such as jump height or sprint time. Inference is what staff think it implies: tissue stress, readiness, "neural fatigue," "healed tissue," injury risk (PDF pp.1-2).
- A force plate can say a jump changed; it cannot say the central nervous system is compromised. GPS can say external work changed; it cannot say what stress the tissue experienced (PDF p.2).
- Humans are redundant systems. The same output can hide a different strategy, so the question is never only "did they hit the number?" but "how did they hit the number, and what happens when we expose them again?" (PDF p.2).
- Matching a previous NordBord score is a valuable data point, not a clearance decision by itself (PDF p.3). The fix is triangulation plus probabilistic language.

### Lab 2B: Capability and Workflow Audit (video 4:35; PDF 3 pp.)

- Small environments align naturally because everyone talks daily. As staff, tools, and handoffs grow, "alignment must be designed, not hoped for" (PDF p.1).
- Capability audit is "tool truth": what it measures, what it does not measure, where its output turns into inference. Workflow audit is where most departments fail: who captures, how it is processed (vendor, in-house code, SpeedSig, dashboards), who interprets, how it is communicated, where the decision gets made (PDF p.1).
- Strategy is the highway (direction, standards, key questions). Tactics are lane changes (which tool, how to adjust tests, timing, exposure). The goal is tactical freedom inside strategic alignment; the video calls this leading by strategic intent and links it to special forces leadership (PDF pp.1-2; transcript ~01:08).
- The payoff is a leadership asset: clarity and onboarding for staff, discipline for the department, a clean budget argument for what is missing, and documented procedures for performance review (PDF p.3).
- The matrix is repeatable and travels with you across clubs; technologies change over time but not overnight (PDF p.3).

### Lab 2C: Monitoring vs Testing (video 8:13; full and Free Version are byte-identical; PDF 3 pp.)

- Monitoring is short-term (days to weeks) and asks "has something changed right now?" It informs load adjustments, recovery, exposure progression or regression, and short-term risk. "Monitoring is status and trend" (PDF p.1).
- Testing is longer reach (weeks to months) and asks "have we improved capacity across a training phase?" Pre-season start vs end, block one vs block two, year one vs year five. "Testing is progress" (PDF p.1).
- Do not misuse methods. Rolling averages and exponentially weighted moving averages are good at "is the athlete drifting from baseline this week?" but not at phase-to-phase change; because the reference moves with the data, a slow decay never falls outside the bounds of normal (PDF pp.1-2; transcript ~02:13). Long-term change needs pre vs post or block vs block comparisons; the video mentions something as simple as an ANOVA (transcript ~02:56).
- The procedure rule: start with the quality you want to evaluate, decide whether you are monitoring or testing, then choose the technology, then assign it to a schedule. "We have force plates, so we should jump" is technology-led practice and creates noise (PDF p.2).
- Communicate to coaches before pressure arrives using five questions: what are we evaluating, why, how often, what output will you receive, what will we do if it changes. "For this time commitment, here's what you get back" (PDF p.2). The video adds a margin-of-error example from AFL time trials: a two-second miss inside known reliable-change error does not trigger extra training (transcript ~06:04).
- For aspiring leaders, the video says this belongs in a "first 90 plan" for a new role (transcript ~04:48). It also references the data, information, knowledge, wisdom ladder as the paradigm for what gets pushed up to coaches (transcript ~05:22).

### Lab 2D: Decision Gates (video 4:46; PDF "Designing Decision Gates", 3 pp.)

- A decision gate is a predefined checkpoint in a workflow where agreed criteria are reviewed and a clear call is made before progressing: Go / Modify / Stop. Gates stop departments from "dumping data" on coaches and senior medical staff and hoping everyone interprets it the same way (PDF p.1).
- Decision gates already exist in everything a department does; the point is to design and control them so they create clarity instead of random data followed by a random response (transcript ~00:49).
- The most common failure is vagueness. "Hamstring injury" or "hamstring capacity" is not a gate; "eccentric knee flexor strength" or "sprint exposure tolerance at a defined speed band and volume" is (PDF p.1).
- Rules agreed before the pressure arrives reduce debate, especially around selection, when emotion enters the room (PDF p.2; transcript ~03:04).
- Timeframes are part of the gate. Different sports have different realities: an NFL-scale organisation may get imaging straight off the field; a lower-funded program may wait days. Set expectations early so timelines are not improvised after an injury (PDF p.2; transcript ~03:29).
- The video's framing: a gate is not just a number, it is a pathway with temporal control; "discipline equals freedom" (transcript ~04:09).

### Lab 2E: The Critical Math That Cannot Be Ignored (video 5:16; PDF 3 pp.)

- Technology provides measurement; the system provides interpretation. The one question technology has to answer with confidence is "is this change real, or is it noise?" Without the math you can collect data but cannot interpret it responsibly or build gates that hold under pressure (PDF p.1).
- Two paths: system-level reliability (can we trust the test at all?) and individual-level monitoring sensitivity (can we detect meaningful change in this athlete?) (PDF p.1).
- Reliability is the whole system, not the device: equipment, protocol, tester, environment, and the athlete's execution (PDF p.1).
- MDC answers "is it beyond noise?" SWC answers "is it worth caring about?" Both matter and serve different purposes (PDF p.1).
- Rate of force development is the classic noisy metric because execution consistency, onset detection choices, and small timing differences all move the number. When a metric is noisy: widen thresholds, tighten the protocol, or choose a more stable metric for gates (PDF p.2). The video's anecdote is a physio arriving with "RFD is off by 12%" when 12% sits well inside the MDC (transcript ~04:13).
- Leadership angle: if staff use tests with unknown reliability, there is no foundation for trust in any number they bring you. Rigour gives credibility, consistent reporting, defensible thresholds, and gates that work (PDF p.2).

### Podcast 2: Evidence Stacking (audio 18:21; PDF "Do We Have Sufficient Information to Act?", SpeedSig/OBP companion blog, 4 pp.)

- Reframes the series question from "how much is enough to act?" to "do we have sufficient information to act?" The most dangerous decisions in high performance are the fastest ones (PDF p.1).
- A signal can be anything: a mechanism on video, a player's reaction, a clinical test, a scan, a hop distance, a single device metric, a coach's comment, or the club's own recent injury history. The mistake is treating any one of them as the verdict (PDF p.1).
- Case 1: a professional soccer forward with bilateral ACL history has an ugly valgus mechanism on video, plays the second half, gets called "out, ACL" by staff primed by recent ACL injuries at the club, then stacks MRI with no reported ACL damage, a full hop within about 12 hours, a known 6.2 m three-hop baseline repeated four times, agility passes, and training at pace. He failed one of six checks and progressed (PDF pp.1-3).
- Case 2: an AFL hamstring three weeks before finals, doctors say "no chance," the high performance manager says "stop, one step at a time," next-day walking and range of motion are good, radiology is inconclusive, and a pre-injury SpeedSig running profile lets them confirm at 5.5 m/s that he is running the same way as before injury. He returned and did not miss another game until the team exited finals (PDF p.3); the podcast adds, hedged with "I think," that he missed the first final (transcript ~17:04).
- Lesson from case 2: the gap is often gym testing to field performance, and generic GPS alone will not answer the "how" question (PDF p.3).
- Leadership: coaches want certainty, staff feel pressure, doctors and physios are human, recent injuries distort judgement, a run of similar injuries can create a false sense of a trend. In unstable environments (new staff, preseason in a week) the leader may need to say "this is how we will proceed; we'll refine it together" (PDF p.3).

## Frameworks and tools taught

### 1. Measurement, Inference, Probability, Next Step (Lab 2A)

What it is: a four-part communication structure that replaces absolutes ("he's ready," "this shows neural fatigue") with labelled inference.

How to run it (PDF pp.3-4):
1. What we measured (facts). Name the tests and the direction of each result.
2. What it suggests (inference). Label it as inference.
3. How confident we are (probability). Say whether probability is improving, stable, or falling.
4. What we recommend next (progression or exposure plan).

Worked example from the PDF (p.4): "We measured five markers associated with hamstring function and running exposure. All are stable pre-to-post and again at 24 hours. Probability is improving that he is ready for the next level of exposure. Next step: controlled progression toward match demands."

The video's one-line axiom (transcript ~05:50): report what you measure, state what you infer, assign a probability, then recommend the next exposure.

What it produces: a coach-facing statement that cannot be accused of over-claiming what the tool knows.

### 2. Triangulation plan (Lab 2A)

What it is: building a case for readiness from multiple angles instead of one test returning to baseline.

Hamstring return-to-play example (PDF p.3): eccentric knee flexor strength; isometric posterior-chain strength; running exposure up to meaningful speed; movement mechanics checks where available; post-exposure response immediately and at 24 hours. The video adds isometrics at inner and outer range and at the hip, jump and hop tests on a force plate for stretch-shortening cycle, and a running mechanics profile to confirm the athlete is achieving speed in an expected way (transcript ~04:13).

Rule: if all tests are positive, exposures are tolerated, and performance holds after load, then the probability improves that the athlete is ready to progress. Probability improves is not certainty (PDF p.3).

What it produces: a 4-6 data-point plan per injury type with a built-in post-exposure check.

### 3. Capability and Workflow Matrix (Lab 2B)

What it is: a one-page grid that maps every technology to the questions it answers and the workflow that carries its output to a decision.

How to build it (PDF p.2):
1. Rows = technologies. List everything: computer and software stack, GPS/IMU, force plates, load cells and force transducers, linear transducers, video tools, wellness and subjective measures.
2. Columns = applications. Option A by domain (rehab, performance, return-to-play, monitoring). Option B by question (hamstring injury, calf injury, adductor/groin, speed development, maximum strength, deceleration ability, fatigue monitoring).
3. Fill each cell with four items: Purpose (what question it answers), Output (the metric or report delivered), Owner (who is responsible), Workflow (capture, process, interpret, communicate, decision).

The video splits Owner further: who owns the capture, who owns the understanding and determines reliability, who maintains the upkeep (transcript ~02:31).

Worked cells (PDF pp.2-3):
- Hamstring rehab (triangulation workflow): force transducer or dynamometry gives a strength capacity trend; GPS/IMU gives exposure dose (high-speed work, accelerations); mechanics check gives strategy change vs baseline; response checks give immediate and 24-hour stability. Workflow names who runs the test, where the data lives, who processes it, how it is reported, who makes the progression decision. The video's version: physio owns capture, sports science owns the reporting template (transcript ~02:59).
- Deceleration capacity (performance workflow): GPS/IMU captures high-intensity deceleration events; data may need processing in Python, R, or SpeedSig; output is a trend report plus exposure tolerance summary; decision is programming adjustment (load, density, drill selection).

What it produces: a matrix, plus a list of gaps (questions you cannot currently answer), bottlenecks (where workflow breaks), and handoff risks (where communication fails). The video's closing test, as best the transcript can be read: if it is not in the matrix it is not in the workflow, and if it is not in the workflow it does not exist (transcript ~04:12, wording garbled).

### 4. Monitoring vs Testing procedure rule (Lab 2C)

What it is: an ordering rule that prevents technology-led practice.

Steps (PDF p.2; transcript ~03:32):
1. Start with the quality you want to evaluate (what capacity matters for this sport, coach, phase, athlete).
2. Decide whether you are monitoring it (short-term status, days to weeks) or testing it (phase change, weeks to months), or both at different times.
3. Choose the technology.
4. Assign it to a schedule inside the periodised plan. Do not make it random. Injury programs should state in advance when testing happens, with flexibility for acute availability questions.
5. Match the analysis to the horizon: rolling averages and EWMA for short-term drift; pre vs post or block vs block comparisons for phase change.

What it produces: definitions of monitoring and testing, and for each key quality a stated horizon, frequency, and output.

### 5. Coach communication script (Lab 2C)

What it is: a five-question brief to run with a new coach or staff group before data collection starts (PDF p.2).

- What are we evaluating?
- Why are we evaluating it?
- How often will we do it?
- What will you receive as output?
- What will we do if it changes?

The video's script form (transcript ~05:31): "We're evaluating X because of Y. We'll do it this often. This is when the test will occur. I'll get the information to you in this period. If we get this result, this is what we're going to do." Include margin of error so a small miss is not treated as meaningful.

What it produces: coach expectations set before a surprise result creates pressure.

### 6. Decision matrix (Lab 2C)

What it is: the bridge from a result to an action. Format (PDF p.2): if we get this result, we do these steps, owned by these people, reviewed at this time point.

Hamstring example (PDF p.2): if eccentric knee flexor force drops meaningfully, confirm test quality and re-test; physio screen plus range-of-motion checks as indicated; adjust exposure plan; reassess response immediately and at 24 hours; progress only when stable. The video's version assigns owners (S&C and sports science confirm the test; physio does clinical strain, ROM, palpation; the S&C coach adjusts the exposure plan for 48 to 72 hours; recheck within 24 hours) (transcript ~07:00). The two versions differ slightly on timing; treat them as illustrative, not as a protocol.

What it produces: for one quality, an "if improves" action, an "if declines" action, owners for each step, and a re-check time.

### 7. Five-part Decision Gate (Lab 2D)

What it is: a predefined checkpoint with agreed criteria and a forced decision (Go / Modify / Stop).

The five parts (PDF pp.1-2):
1. What is being evaluated. Name the capacity and the contraction or task precisely: eccentric knee flexor strength, isometric hip extension strength, sprint exposure tolerance (defined speed band and volume), deceleration exposure tolerance (defined intensity and count).
2. Criteria. Pass (green): proceed. Fail (red): stop or regress. Borderline (amber): confirm, repeat, or add another data point. Also define what counts as a breach so people do not argue afterwards. The video adds that criteria must be statistically grounded: different to this person, to their history, and to the population (transcript ~01:46).
3. Decision options. Progress, Hold, Regress, Refer (to medical lead), Escalate (specialist imaging or surgical opinion). Options should reflect the sport and medical setup.
4. Ownership. Who provides inputs, who interprets results, who owns the final call. Performance and medical staff often share inputs but one role owns the decision, especially in return-to-play progression.
5. Next step. Every gate triggers immediate action with a time window. PDF examples: pass, progress to next exposure stage; fail, regress and re-test in 72 hours; borderline, repeat test plus add another measure and set the review time.

Timeframes are built in (PDF p.2): "First clinical review happens within X hours. Imaging is expected within Y days if criteria are met. First progression gate occurs on Day Z, assuming symptoms and function allow."

What it produces: two written gates (one performance, one rehab) each with all five parts.

### 8. Reliability and threshold concepts (Lab 2E)

What it is: the minimum statistical vocabulary underneath every gate. The course teaches definitions and a decision rule; it does not present computational formulas.

Path 1, system-level reliability (PDF p.1):
- ICC (intraclass correlation coefficient): how consistently athletes are ranked across repeated trials. Relative reliability.
- SEM / TE (standard error of measurement / typical error): the size of the noise in the units you care about. Absolute reliability. "SEM/TE tells you how noisy the test is."
- MDC95 (minimal detectable change at 95% confidence): how much change is required to be confident the shift is beyond typical measurement noise. "MDC95 tells you how much change you need before you can call it real."

Path 2, individual-level monitoring sensitivity (PDF p.1):
- Typical error / within-athlete variability, often summarised as CV% for repeated measures.
- SWC (smallest worthwhile change): the smallest change that is practically meaningful, not just statistically real.

Decision logic (PDF p.2; transcript ~03:34):
- Change below MDC95: likely noise.
- Change above MDC95: likely real.
- Change above SWC: likely meaningful.
- Change above both: act with confidence.
- Change real but not meaningful: note it, watch it, do not overreact.
- Neither: treat any difference as noise.

Noisy metric rule (PDF p.2): widen thresholds, tighten the protocol, or choose a more stable metric for gates. RFD is the named example.

Note for staff use: the standard computational formulas for SEM, MDC95, and SWC are not given in the course materials; the lab expects the department to already have or compute these values for its own tests.

### 9. CM² progression: Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum (Podcast 2)

What it is: a defensible step-by-step rehab progression. Start at the base and earn the next step (PDF p.2; transcript ~09:54).

1. Control: single-joint control, range of motion, joint tolerance (effusion, pain behaviour).
2. Movement: sequencing hip, knee, and ankle together; simple patterns before complex.
3. Capacity: clearance tests appropriate to the injury; hops, deceleration, strength outputs.
4. Maximum / Performance: sport-specific exposures; fatigue-resilient execution at relevant pace.

### 10. Six-check Evidence Stack (Podcast 2)

What it is: a checklist to remove emotion and stop a department reacting to one dramatic input. Rule: no single signal decides the outcome (PDF pp.2-4; transcript ~10:45).

1. Mechanism: was there a plausible mechanism, and what does video actually show and not show (load, weight-bearing)?
2. Radiology: use it but it is interpretive; clear structural disruption is clear, tissue "signal" needs context.
3. Clinical exam: range of motion, effusion, functional limp, key ligament tests (anterior drawer endpoint), gait.
4. Fundamental control and movement checks: can they control the joint, can they sequence cleanly?
5. Capacity tests (clearance tests): hops, deceleration, strength and SSC outputs relevant to the tissue and sport.
6. Performance-relevant functional tests: on-field movement, agility and exposure at pace, execution without breakdown under fatigue.

Count passes against fails. In the soccer case the athlete failed one of six and passed the rest, which shifted the decision from fear to probability.

### 11. Statistics-to-decision sequence (Podcast 2 blog)

Five steps (PDF p.3): test your tests (system reliability); build athlete baselines early; define thresholds (normal variation, SWC, what counts as meaningful in your world); use multiple signals; bridge data to decisions so you can say "this is what we saw, this is what it means, this is what we do next." The goal is not perfect certainty but reducing avoidable error.

## Deliverables / exercises

All deliverables are stated in the "Lab task" section of each PDF.

Lab 2A (PDF p.4):
1. A one-paragraph definition: "Technology is an accelerator because..."
2. Three measurements collected weekly, each with what is measured and what is typically inferred.
3. One example where the environment overstates certainty (CMJ fatigue, GPS load, isometrics), rewritten as measurement, inference, probability, next step.
4. A triangulation plan for one injury type (hamstring, groin, calf, knee) using 4-6 data points and a post-exposure check.

Lab 2B (PDF p.3):
1. A one-page Capability and Workflow Matrix (rows = tech, columns = applications).
2. At least 10 cells completed with purpose, output, owner, workflow steps.
3. A list of gaps, bottlenecks, and handoff risks.

Lab 2C (PDF p.3):
1. Written definitions of monitoring and testing.
2. One quality (deceleration capacity, jump performance, hamstring capacity) specified as monitored, tested, or both, with frequency and output.
3. A decision matrix: if result improves, action; if result declines, action; who owns each step; when to re-check.

Lab 2D (PDF p.3):
Two decision gates, one performance (speed exposure progression or deceleration capacity) and one rehab (hamstring return-to-run), each with key quality, pass/fail/borderline criteria, decision options, ownership, and next step plus timeframe.

Lab 2E (PDF p.3):
1. Top 5 tests or metrics, each with ICC (if available), SEM/TE, and MDC95 or chosen decision threshold.
2. For one key monitoring metric: within-athlete variability (TE or CV%) and SWC.
3. One decision gate statement: "If change is > ___, we do ___; if not, we ___."

Podcast 2 blog (PDF pp.3-4):
- The Evidence Stack Card (copy/paste): decision question plus the six checks in order.
- Five reflection prompts: where single-signal decisions happen most in your environment; which of the six checks you skip under pressure; whether you have baseline profiles for key tests; what "one step at a time" looks like for a knee ligament incident, hamstring injury, and groin pain episode; how your evidence stack sounds when explained to a coach in 30 seconds.

## Key quotes

1. "Technology accelerates practice. It does not create practice." (Lab 2a PDF p.1)
2. "A device doesn't create impact. A workflow does." (Lab 2b PDF p.1)
3. "Monitoring is status and trend. Testing is progress." (Lab 2c PDF p.1)
4. "Coaches don't need more numbers. They need clarity." (Lab 2c PDF p.2)
5. "If ownership is unclear, gates become meetings instead of decisions." (Lab 2D PDF p.2)
6. "A gate without a next step is just conversation." (Lab 2D PDF p.2)
7. "SEM/TE tells you how noisy the test is. MDC95 tells you how much change you need before you can call it real." (Lab 2E PDF p.1)
8. "If you can't quantify noise, you can't defend your decisions." (Lab 2E video ~04:57)
9. "Leadership is staying clinical when others can't." (Stacking Evidence blog p.1)
10. "No single signal decides the outcome." (Stacking Evidence blog p.4)

## Source confidence

PDF text extraction: all six PDFs yielded clean text; none were image-only.
- Lab_2a_Blog_What_is_the_Role_of_Technology.pdf: 4 pages, text extracted.
- Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit.pdf: 3 pages, text extracted.
- Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing.pdf: 3 pages, text extracted.
- Lab_2D_Decision_Gates.pdf: 3 pages, text extracted.
- Lab_2E_The_Critcal_Math_that_can_t_be_Ignored.pdf: 3 pages, text extracted.
- Stacking_Evidence_Blog.pdf: 4 pages, text extracted. Branded SpeedSig / OBP and labelled a companion to "Podcast 2 in the Decision to Data series."

Transcript notes: Lab 2C full-course video and the Free Version are byte-identical (SHA-256, per the summary file), so one set of timestamps covers both. The instructor is not named in any transcript or PDF. Transcript misrecognitions corrected against the PDFs: "nofop remote range" = MDC95; "SCMs" = SEM; "NDC" = MDC; "inter-class correlation" = intraclass correlation coefficient; "SpeedCig," "SpeedSeek," "v-sig," "speed-sick" = SpeedSig; "CM squared" = CM² (Control, Movement, Capacity, Maximum); "bicep femteth" = biceps femoris.

Major claims and frameworks:
- Technology as accelerator, not creator: PDF-confirmed (2a p.1). The Jim Collins / Good to Great attribution: transcript-only (2A ~00:39).
- Measurement vs inference lists and the force plate / GPS trap: PDF-confirmed (2a pp.1-2).
- Four-step communication structure and worked hamstring script: PDF-confirmed (2a pp.3-4).
- Triangulation plan for hamstring: PDF-confirmed (2a p.3). Extra tests in the video (inner/outer range isometrics, hip isometrics, hops, running mechanics profile): transcript-only (2A ~04:13).
- NordBord match is not clearance: PDF-confirmed (2a p.3).
- Capability vs workflow definitions, strategy vs tactic: PDF-confirmed (2b p.1). "Leading by strategic intent" and special forces reference: transcript-only (2B ~01:08).
- Matrix build steps, four items per cell, two worked cells: PDF-confirmed (2b pp.2-3). Three-way ownership split (capture, understanding/reliability, upkeep): transcript-only (2B ~02:31).
- Leadership payoffs (onboarding, budget, performance review): PDF-confirmed (2b p.3).
- "If it isn't in the workflow it doesn't exist" closing: transcript-only, garbled (2B ~04:12).
- Monitoring and testing definitions and horizons: PDF-confirmed (2c p.1).
- EWMA misses slow decay: PDF-confirmed in principle (2c pp.1-2); the decay mechanism explanation and ANOVA mention: transcript-only (2C ~02:13, ~02:56).
- Procedure rule (quality, monitor or test, technology, schedule): PDF-confirmed (2c p.2).
- Five coach-communication questions: PDF-confirmed (2c p.2). "First 90 plan," DIKW ladder, AFL time-trial two-second example: transcript-only (2C ~04:48, ~05:22, ~06:04).
- Decision matrix format and hamstring example: PDF-confirmed (2c p.2). Owner assignments and 48-72 hour / 24 hour timings: transcript-only (2C ~07:00).
- Decision gate definition and five parts: PDF-confirmed (2D pp.1-2). "Statistically different to the person, their history, the population": transcript-only (2D ~01:46).
- Pass/fail/borderline with green/red/amber and the 72-hour re-test example: PDF-confirmed (2D pp.1-2).
- Timeframes built into gates: PDF-confirmed (2D p.2). NFL vs lower-funded sport example: transcript-only (2D ~03:29). "Discipline equals freedom": transcript-only (2D ~04:09).
- Two reliability paths, ICC/SEM/TE/MDC95/CV%/SWC definitions: PDF-confirmed (2E p.1).
- MDC/SWC decision logic: PDF-confirmed (2E p.2).
- RFD as noisy metric and three responses: PDF-confirmed (2E p.2). 12% RFD anecdote: transcript-only (2E ~04:13).
- Rigour creates trust: PDF-confirmed (2E p.2).
- Evidence stack framing and signal list: PDF-confirmed (Stacking p.1).
- Soccer case including 6.2 m three-hop repeated four times, MRI signal without damage, hop at ~12 hours: PDF-confirmed (Stacking pp.1-2). Prior full ACL reconstruction plus a more recent left ACL in 2022: PDF-confirmed (p.1); the word "bilateral" is transcript-only (Podcast ~01:38). Semimembranosus graft and hip-lock side story: transcript-only (Podcast ~05:52).
- CM² progression: PDF-confirmed (Stacking p.2).
- Six checks: PDF-confirmed (Stacking pp.2-4).
- AFL hamstring case, 5.5 m/s SpeedSig comparison, returned and did not miss another game until the team exited finals: PDF-confirmed (Stacking p.3). "Missed the first final": transcript-only and hedged by the speaker (Podcast ~17:04).
- Five-step statistics-to-decision sequence: PDF-confirmed (Stacking p.3).
- Leadership in unstable environments ("this is how we will proceed"): PDF-confirmed (Stacking p.3). US college football staff turnover context: transcript-only (Podcast ~09:05).
- Evidence Stack Card and reflection prompts: PDF-confirmed (Stacking pp.3-4).

## Applicability notes

- The Capability and Workflow Matrix maps directly onto the Applied Performance stack. Rows: Catapult GPS, VALD force plates, VALD dynamometry (NordBord, ForceFrame, DynaMo), the AMS, video, wellness. Columns by question the football and Olympic sport coaches actually ask. The matrix exposes the cells where the AMS holds data nobody acts on, and the cells where Athletic Performance captures a metric but Athletic Medicine never sees it. It also doubles as the onboarding document for new Athletic Performance staff and the budget justification for the next VALD or Catapult renewal.
- Lab 2A's NordBord example is a direct warning for VALD reporting: a returning athlete matching their pre-injury eccentric knee flexor score is one data point in a triangulation, not a return-to-play clearance. Athletic Performance and Athletic Medicine should agree that the AMS return-to-play summary reports the measured markers, the inference, the confidence, and the next exposure step rather than a "cleared / not cleared" flag.
- Lab 2C forces a decision about which Catapult and VALD outputs are monitoring and which are testing. Daily CMJ on force plates and session high-speed running from Catapult are monitoring (EWMA and rolling baselines in the AMS are appropriate). Pre-camp vs post-camp or block-to-block strength and jump batteries are testing and need pre vs post comparison, not the AMS's continuous smoothing. Coaches should be told which is which before the season starts, using the five-question script.
- Lab 2E is the technical work the department owes itself. Every VALD and Catapult metric used in a decision gate needs its own ICC, SEM/TE, and MDC95 from Baylor's own equipment, protocol, testers, and environment, plus a within-athlete CV% and SWC for the monitored metrics. Vendor-published reliability is a starting point, not a substitute. Force plate RFD and other early-phase force-time metrics should be treated as noisy until proven otherwise; use wider bands or a more stable metric for gates.
- Decision gates and the decision matrix belong in the AMS as written rules with owners: what quality, what threshold in local MDC and SWC units, what options, who in Athletic Medicine owns the return-to-play call and who in Athletic Performance owns the exposure adjustment, and the re-check window. Writing timeframes into the gate (first clinical review within X hours, imaging within Y days, first progression gate on Day Z) is what stops a head coach's Sunday phone call from setting the timeline.
- The six-check evidence stack is a shared language for Athletic Performance and Athletic Medicine case reviews after an in-game incident. Mechanism from film, radiology, clinical exam, control and movement, capacity tests on VALD, and performance-relevant field exposure on Catapult give both groups a structured way to say "we have five of six" instead of reacting to the clip. The AFL case shows why a pre-injury running profile from GPS matters: the return-to-run question is not only "can he hit 5.5 m/s" but "is he running the same way he did before."
