1	# Module 4: The Integration Problem (Data to Decisions)
2	
3	Numbering note: the course materials label this block internally as "Module 6" (Section 1 / 6A, 6B Part A and B, 6E, Podcast 6). The lecturer is Dr Jason Weber (Old Bull Performance). Eric's Drive folder calls it Module 4 and that number is used here. Where the video says "Module 6C" it is the file titled 6D The Decision Pathway; where it says "6B Part 2" it is 6C The Translation Problem.
4	
5	The module's argument is that technically strong practitioners fail to influence decisions not because they lack knowledge but because the department has no operating model that carries information from collection to action. Weber names five places where that chain breaks (language, decision pathway, authority, relationship, process), then goes deeper on two of them: the encoding problem (each discipline reads the same athlete through a different lens) and the translation problem (someone is permanently re-explaining the basics, which is a leadership failure disguised as a communication chore). He then makes the pathway explicit as six stages with five audit points, and applies the whole thing to the physio to strength-and-conditioning overlap he calls the grey zone, which must be profiled, owned, gated and communicated rather than left to personality. The closing podcast argues that once a department is aligned, the new risk is groupthink, so leaders need structured dissent built into the decision log. The through-line is Weber's own confession: he had the right data on bone stress risk and the injuries he predicted happened anyway, because he had not made the information consumable to the doctor and the coach in advance.
6	
7	## Lessons
8	
9	### Video Lab 6A: The Integration Problem (15:42), with 6A Summary PDF, Integration Cheat Sheet PDF, Integration Problem Workbook PDF
10	
11	- The failure mode: a data-literate, sharp practitioner whose recommendations are ignored, diluted or not understood. "It's typically not a knowledge problem, it's an integration problem" (00:01:00).
12	- Warning signs (00:01:20 to 00:04:22): no upward pathway; other departments do not understand you; junior staff unaware they are stage one of five; terminology confusion; a dismissive domain owner; philosophical differences in models.
13	- Four self-audit questions and five integration breakpoints (00:05:54 to 00:13:07); see Frameworks 1 and 2.
14	- On authority: make the call, but explain it in the meeting and again privately, and let the argument run rather than shutting it down (00:08:41 to 00:10:20).
15	- Weber's confession: bone stress data was not "medically friendly", the coach deferred to a doctor who did not understand it, and the predicted injuries arrived six weeks later (00:14:05 to 00:15:10).
16	
17	### Video Lab 6B: The Encoding Problem (16:23), with Module_6B_Part_A PDF
18	
19	- Disciplines encode the same facts differently: physio sees tissue tolerance, medical sees health risk, strength staff see outputs, sport science sees load, the coach sees availability. Nobody disagrees on the facts, only on what they mean (00:00:23 to 00:01:28; PDF p.1).
20	- Realigning the encoding framework is the core leadership job and requires written scenario pre-commitment ("when we get A, this is what we do"); see Framework 4.
21	- The health indicator of alignment: staff know what each other will do next, so nobody withholds an opinion or a handover (00:04:46 to 00:06:07; PDF p.1).
22	- Reasoned technical challenge is welcome; working outside the agreed process is not. The physio who ran an unplanned maximal eccentric test the day before a game, after which the player tore, is the cautionary case (00:06:38 to 00:09:31; PDF p.2).
23	- SOPs reveal who can operate inside a collaborative system; the SEC football example and first-meeting script are the model for inheriting a divided department (00:09:33 to 00:12:22; PDF p.2); see Framework 5.
24	- "As a technician I probably did a good job, but as a leader I didn't" (00:14:27): the doctor called the bone stress data "not an MRI".
25	
26	### Video Lab 6C: The Translation Problem (13:04), with Module_6B_Part_B PDF
27	
28	- Translation is the daily cost of unresolved encoding: explaining the same issue to medical, strength, physio, then coach. A "performance leak" (PDF p.1) and a threat to "cognitive survivability" (00:07:24).
29	- "Avoid translation, focus on education, and focus on it early" (00:02:25). Constant re-explanation is diagnostic evidence that the system is not aligned (PDF p.1).
30	- Two routes (line in the sand, or workshops and internal CPD) and the Option A / Option B leadership choice; see Framework 6.
31	- Contested metrics (eccentric hamstring is the example) need an agreed place in the framework before high-level meetings (00:06:12 to 00:07:21; PDF p.2).
32	- Worked case: pelvic control in stance was framed as a strength deficit; isometric abduction showed athletes were strong enough and the problem was motor control. A line in the sand drawn with evidence, not authority (00:08:30 to 00:10:58; PDF p.2 to p.3).
33	
34	### Video Lab 6D: The Decision Pathway (12:14), no companion PDF
35	
36	- Every significant decision travels six stages with five failure points between them, each with an audit question (00:01:06 to 00:10:50); see Framework 7.
37	- Communication example: "moderate signal, want to be cautious" lands with a coach as "no recommendation", when the practitioner meant "reduce intensity 15%" (00:06:27).
38	- The 20-second rule: lead with the recommendation, not the method or the number (00:07:46). Weber guards the channel between his level and the head coach (00:07:08).
39	- Authority example: physio recommends no contact, coach agrees, 20 minutes later the athlete is in full contact with no recorded override. Keep written notes (00:09:11 to 00:10:34).
40	- The highest-friction failure point is usually the one closest to stage six, where consequences are visible (00:11:09).
41	
42	### Video Lab 6E: The Grey Zone (13:15), with Grey Zone Workbook PDF and Grey Zone Summary PDF
43	
44	- The grey zone is where physio and strength staff work on the same athlete from different timelines, risk tolerances and definitions. It exists everywhere; the problem is it has not been structured, so people default to assumption (00:00:22 to 00:01:35; Summary p.1).
45	- People before process: profile everyone in the interface on the Knowledge-Behaviour Matrix, because the same model works with one pair and fails with another (00:02:44 to 00:03:59; Summary p.2).
46	- One operational logic, not medical and performance logics in parallel, agreed before measurement influences the pathway (00:03:59 to 00:05:28; Summary p.3).
47	- Phase ownership, empowerment levels and communication rules (00:05:34 to 00:10:43); "wearing the S&C badge" does not mean you can coach running; see Framework 8.
48	- The walkthrough exercise: tell one case twice, physio's eyes then S&C's, find the divergence points, write an integration protocol for each (00:10:43 to 00:12:12).
49	
50	### Podcast 6: Structured Thinking Under Pressure (14:04), with Structured_Thinking_Under_Pressure PDF
51	
52	- "Seeing around corners" requires stepping out of the processes you built (working on the business, not in it) and asking, bluntly, what could derail this (00:00:41 to 00:02:02).
53	- The 10th Man Rule from World War Z is dramatised but real (Israel's Devil's Advocate Unit, post-1973). Once everyone is "playing nicely in the sandpit", groupthink is the new risk (00:02:02 to 00:04:37; PDF p.1 to p.2).
54	- Most technology infers an outcome rather than measuring it; do not let the group agree its way past that (00:04:06).
55	- Meeting techniques: the rugby coach who sits silent then asks questions designed to unravel the plan; "five minutes, data only, no grand final pressure" (00:05:04 to 00:07:32).
56	- The AFL calf case: recurrent fatigue tears the coach understood intellectually but not emotionally; the fix was the doctor saying "stop everything", a different messenger for the same conclusion (00:08:04 to 00:10:00).
57	- A working system must be re-reviewed as staff, technology and knowledge change (00:11:57 to 00:13:42); see Framework 9.
58	
59	## Frameworks and tools taught
60	
61	### 1. The Five Integration Breakpoints (6A; Cheat Sheet p.1; Workbook p.4; 6A Summary p.1)
62	
63	A diagnostic for any past decision where sound technical work did not change the outcome. Tick which broke: (1) Language gap: no shared framework for status, readiness or risk, including philosophical gaps where the words are understood but the models differ. (2) Decision pathway gap: no pre-agreed route for who collects, who reviews, where it goes next, what triggers a conversation. (3) Authority gradient: a senior figure overrides sound input without challenge or explanation. (4) Relationship deficit: the decision maker does not trust or understand the source; Weber treats this as the practitioner's responsibility to pre-educate. (5) Process absence: no meeting, gate or checkpoint requires the input to be addressed before the decision is finalised. Product: a named breakpoint for a specific case, plus what would have needed to be different.
64	
65	### 2. The Diagnostic Questions (Workbook p.2; 6A 00:05:54)
66	
67	Ask of yourself or each staff member: (1) When did your data last directly change a coaching decision? If none in three months, that is the answer. Trace the pathway. (2) How many people could accurately explain what the monitoring system measures and why? Estimate, name the gaps by role, state the cost. (3) What happens to your recommendations when you are not in the room: hold, modified, or disappear? (4, video only) How many could explain the return-to-run model and its decision gates?
68	
69	### 3. The Real-World Failure Case reflection (Integration Workbook p.1 to p.5)
70	
71	Sections A to E in order. A: define the integration problem as it appears in your environment; rate frequency (rarely / occasionally / regularly / almost always) and describe one observable signal. C: one case where technical quality was sound but the process produced a poor outcome: context and people; what the data indicated; what was decided instead and what overrode it; downstream cost to athlete, team, credibility, department. Optional table for multiple cases (Situation / What the data said / What happened instead / Downstream cost). D: locate the break against the five breakpoints; one-off or recurring and what has blocked resolution; what would have needed to be different (a process, relationship, language, structure or moment). E: complete "The one integration failure in my current environment that I most need to resolve is..." and bring it to the live session. The workbook states the rest of the module is built as responses to this case.
72	
73	### 4. Encoding Realignment by scenario pre-commitment (6B; Part A PDF p.1)
74	
75	Pick a common presentation (Weber uses a grade 2A hamstring). Before it happens, with every discipline in the room, write: how it will be assessed; the checkpoints; day-by-day expectations and tempo; the realistic return-to-performance timeline; who acts at each handover (for example day four to running staff); criteria for adapting off the plan. The output is a document the staff built together, which is what the coach sees ("this is the plan, these are the checkpoints"), and which is the reference for judging whether a deviation is a reasoned challenge or someone working outside the system. Repeat for performance progressions. Health check: can the physio describe what the strength coach will do next week, and vice versa.
76	
77	### 5. First-meeting operating statement and SOPs (6B 00:11:43 to 00:12:22; Part A PDF p.2)
78	
79	When inheriting a department, the first group meeting sets the encoding framework: who you are, what you do, how the department will operate, that you were hired to install a system rather than remove people, and that everyone will work to it. SOPs follow and are positioned as the way to find out who can work inside a collaborative system, and the transparent basis for escalating anyone who cannot.
80	
81	### 6. The Translation Audit and the Option A / Option B choice (6C; Part B PDF p.1 to p.2)
82	
83	List every concept you re-explain to a second and third audience in the same week; each is a gap. For each gap choose the route: line in the sand or education through workshops and internal CPD. Decide honestly who teaches it: Option A, you have the technical depth and stand up and explain the framework; Option B, you hire or empower the person who does and trust them, and do not defer to someone because it is easy. Agree in advance how contested metrics are framed in this environment. Product: an education plan sized to the resources you actually have.
84	
85	### 7. The Six-Stage Decision Pathway and Five-Point Audit (6D, transcript only)
86	
87	Stages: (1) data capture: GPS, force plate, RPE, clinical assessment, observation; (2) quality control: protocol followed, conditions consistent, anomalies caught; (3) analysis: thresholds, baselines; (4) interpretation: this number means the athlete is in this state; (5) communication: presenting to the person who acts; (6) decision and action.
88	
89	Failure points and audit questions:
90	
91	1. Dirty data (between 1 and 2). Unit not worn correctly, plate not zeroed, protocol skipped, and it sits in the database for weeks. Ask: who owns quality control and what does the check specifically consist of? If the answer is "nobody, it's informal", that is the finding.
92	2. Expertise gap (between 2 and 3). Data reliable but the analyst lacks the framework: normal-limit changes flagged as severe, a 50 ms RFD change on shoulder external rotation treated as an emergency. Ask: who set the thresholds, where were the defaults inherited from, is it written in a software platform, who reviews it, and is there a high-clarity handover when staff change?
93	3. Interpretation gap (between 3 and 4). A number is reported and the meeting moves on. Often caused by collecting more than the system can process. Ask: does it stop at the number, and who is there to handle it?
94	4. Communication gap (between 4 and 5). Technically precise, operationally opaque. Ask: what do you lead with, the method, the number or the recommendation? Apply the 20-second rule and a pre-built delivery structure for the coach.
95	5. Authority gap (between 5 and 6). Clear recommendation, no gate, never becomes a decision. Ask: is there a pre-agreed process that requires technical input to be formally addressed before return to play or selection is finalised? If not, recommendations are "advisory at best, optional at worst".
96	
97	Product: name the single failure point costing the most decision quality each week (not the one that implicates someone) and fix it first. Keep written notes on every recommendation and decision.
98	
99	### 8. The Grey Zone build, seven steps (6E; Grey Zone Workbook p.1 to p.12; Grey Zone Summary p.2 to p.7)
100	
101	Run in order; the diagnostic leads into the design, which leads into the operating protocols.
102	
103	Step 1, People Profile (Workbook p.2 to p.3). Map every staff member in the physio-S&C interface: Knowledge level (Handbrake: low knowledge, defaults to assumption, needs close supervision; Pawn: has knowledge but relies on instruction, hesitates at transitions; Practitioner: competent in own domain, collaboration depends on openness; Operator: high knowledge, autonomous, check for territorial bias) crossed with Behaviour (Misaligned: works against departmental logic; Coaster: present but passive under pressure; Catalyst: drives collaboration, anchor your protocols here; Beacon: sets the standard, amplifies or, if misaligned, undermines). Combinations needing extra structure: Misaligned x Operator; Beacon (Misaligned) x any Handbrake; two Practitioners with different domain biases; Pawn S&C + Operator Physio. Combinations that self-organise: Beacon x Catalyst; Operator x Operator with explicit handover points; Catalyst x Practitioner. Write the biggest risk in this specific pairing and the level of structure it needs.
104	
105	Step 2, One Operational Logic (Workbook p.4; Summary p.3). Facilitate and record the agreed position (not individual opinions) on six domains: hamstring rehab markers; running readiness criteria (quality of movement versus quantity of exposure); return to full training threshold (what tests, who signs off); data we trust in-house; data we do not act on in isolation; what "athlete ready" means. Leave a row blank if unresolved; the blank is the priority.
106	
107	Step 3, Rehab Phase Ownership Map (Workbook p.5; Summary p.4). For Return to Function (acute / post-surgical), Return to Run (loading), Return to Play (performance rebuild), Return to Competition: who owns it, who contributes, transition criteria, escalation required. Weber's reference: medical/physio owns RTF with S&C running parallel conditioning ("physio controls direction, S&C does not wait"); S&C owns RTR in most environments unless an exceptional running physio changes the calculus; RTP shared per pre-agreed criteria; RTC department-lead sign-off with immediate communication to the head coach. Pre-agree before any athlete is injured.
108	
109	Step 4, Cross-Check Method (6E 00:07:43; Summary p.4). Even when S&C owns the phase, ask the physio to account for it. If the physio can relay the rationale, communication happened; if not, it did not. This is how you verify the model is running rather than assumed.
110	
111	Step 5, Decision Empowerment Checklist (Workbook p.6; Summary p.5). For seven decision types (progress loading within agreed programme; regress loading; remove athlete from a field session; modify a published session; progress to next rehab phase; seek external specialist referral; return athlete to full contact) mark Yes/No for physio can act, S&C can act, must escalate to department lead. Skipping this produces overreach (Operator knowledge without role boundaries) or paralysis (Pawn behaviour in a Practitioner role, holding athletes back waiting for permission never withheld).
112	
113	Step 6, Communication Protocol (Workbook p.7; Summary p.5 to p.6). For each decision event (athlete removed from field session; phase progressed; phase regressed or paused; specialist referral; return to full training cleared) fill in who is told, how fast, via what channel. Rules: the operationally responsible person owns the communication; the list is pre-defined per decision type; anything touching field presence is immediate, not end of session, not email; escalation triggers are pre-agreed so escalation is never a surprise. Then write the single biggest communication failure point and the one protocol change that fixes it.
114	
115	Step 7, Walkthrough Exercise (Workbook p.8 to p.9; Summary p.6 to p.7). Choose one real or well-built hypothetical case. Physio and S&C coach each answer, in front of each other: what does progress look like; key risks right now; what data do you trust; time constraints; where do you need the other discipline most; what would cause you to pause or regress. Mark two or three divergence points. For the top one write the integration protocol: who owns this moment; what criteria determine the outcome; what is handed over and to whom; who can change the programme; who must be informed; what goes to the department lead without exception.
116	
117	Finish with the Grey Zone Master Checklist (Workbook p.10 to p.11): 22 boxes across People Diagnosis, Operational Logic, Phase Ownership, Decision Empowerment, Communication, Ongoing Operations. "A blank box is a structural risk." Re-run after any staff change or mid-season.
118	
119	### 9. Structured dissent toolkit (Podcast 6; Structured Thinking PDF p.1 to p.8)
120	
121	- 10th Man Rule: when consensus forms, one person has the formal, protected obligation to argue the opposite. OBP application: designate that voice in the Kaigi decision log before RTR or programme calls are logged (PDF p.6).
122	- Six Thinking Hats (de Bono): White facts only; Red gut feel without justification; Black what could go wrong (the 10th Man hat); Yellow best case; Green alternative paths; Blue process control, who owns the decision and what is the review trigger. Everyone wears the same hat at the same time (PDF p.2 to p.3). Weber's lightweight version: "five minutes, data only".
123	- Pre-Mortem (Klein / Kahneman), three steps: state the decision; project forward ("it is four weeks from now, he is re-injured, what happened?") with each person writing independently before discussion; collect and group the failure scenarios and use the most credible to add contingencies before committing (PDF p.3).
124	- System 1 / System 2: Go/No-Go and Kaigi exist to force slow thinking onto decisions staff would otherwise make on pattern recognition, especially when a situation looks familiar but is not (PDF p.4).
125	- Red Teaming, five questions: under what conditions does this monitoring system give false confidence; what would have to be true about this athlete for our RTR assessment to be wrong; where are we relying on a single source; what are we not measuring and does the decision assume it is fine; if a different department looked at this data what would they conclude. Inter-departmental version: medical reviews performance decisions, S&C stress-tests medical thresholds (PDF p.4 to p.6).
126	- OODA loop: orientation (the department's "concept") is the underrated failure stage; accurate data through a stale filter still gives a wrong decision. Ask when you last reoriented your monitoring assumptions (PDF p.5 to p.6).
127	- OBP Bias Prompt Analysis, four layers to run before a decision is logged (PDF p.6 to p.7): (1) Recognition: what do we know, facts only; (2) Assumption audit: what are we treating as stable that might not be, when did we last check our concept; (3) Inversion: assign a 10th Man to argue the opposite and record the argument; (4) Pre-mortem close: "if this decision is wrong in four weeks, what happened?", record the top two answers in the decision log as review triggers.
128	
129	## Deliverables / exercises
130	
131	1. Integration Problem Workbook (5 pages): sections A to E per Framework 3, ending with the one-sentence closing statement for the live session.
132	2. Translation gap identification: 6C (00:02:31) refers to "the workbook associated with this lab". No such workbook is in the course folder; the Part B PDF is prose. Framework 6 is the reconstruction.
133	3. Decision Pathway audit (6D, 00:10:52 to 00:12:11): trace one recent important decision through all six stages, name the costliest failure point, assign an owner and a specific check. No PDF accompanies this lab.
134	4. Grey Zone Workbook (12 pages): People Profile and combination check (p.3); Operational Logic table (p.4); Rehab Phase Ownership Map (p.5); Decision Empowerment Checklist (p.6); Communication Protocol (p.7); Walkthrough table and divergence points (p.8 to p.9); Master Checklist (p.10 to p.11). Complete the People Profile first; design for the real environment; revisit after any staff change.
135	5. Structured Thinking: watch World War Z as a priming device (podcast 00:13:36; PDF p.6), then run the four-layer Bias Prompt Analysis on a live return-to-play or programme decision and record the review triggers. The PDF closes with: what is your department's current concept, when did you last audit it, how old is the filter you run monitoring data through (p.8).
136	
137	## Key quotes
138	
139	- "It's typically not a knowledge problem. It's an integration problem." (6A, 00:01:00)
140	- "It's not just about what I can do. It's about what I can get my team to do." (6A, 00:11:59)
141	- "If your recommendation changes as it moves up the chain, there is likely an integration leak." (Integration Cheat Sheet, p.1)
142	- "As a technician, I probably did a good job, but as a leader, I didn't." (6B, 00:14:27)
143	- "Translation is not just inconvenient. It is a performance leak inside the organisation." (Module 6B Part B PDF, p.1)
144	- "If you're more than 20 seconds away from getting an actual recommendation or coach, it's going to be lost." (6D, 00:07:56; transcript wording)
145	- "Otherwise, recommendations become advisory at best and optional at worst." (6D, 00:10:43)
146	- "The gray zone is not something we eliminate. It's something we organise." (6E, 00:12:16; also Grey Zone Workbook p.1)
147	- "Unowned zones always fill with assumption." (Grey Zone Workbook, p.12)
148	- "Don't wait for someone brave enough to raise the concern. Build the mechanism that makes raising it expected, protected, and logged." (Structured Thinking PDF, p.7)
149	
150	## Source confidence
151	
152	PDF extraction: all eight PDFs yielded full text (pypdf). None were image-only. The Grey Zone Workbook (12 pages) was additionally read as page images because of the Read tool's 10-page limit; its text layer also extracted cleanly, so page references are reliable.
153	
154	| PDF | Pages | Text extracted |
155	|---|---|---|
156	| The_Leader_s_Integration_Cheat_Sheet.pdf | 1 | Yes |
157	| The_Integration_Problem_Workbook.pdf | 5 | Yes |
158	| Video_Lab_6A_Summary_-_The_Integration_Problem.pdf | 1 | Yes |
159	| Module_6B_Part_A_-_The_Encoding_Problem.pdf | 3 | Yes |
160	| Module_6B_Part_B_-_The_Translation_Problem.pdf | 3 | Yes |
161	| Structured_Thinking_Under_Pressure.pdf | 8 | Yes |
162	| The_Grey_Zone_Workbook.pdf | 12 | Yes (also read as images) |
163	| Video_Lab_The_Grey_Zone_Summary.pdf | 8 | Yes |
164	
165	By framework:
166	
167	- Five breakpoints: PDF-confirmed (Cheat Sheet p.1; Workbook p.4; 6A Summary p.1). The explain-in-meeting-and-again-privately handling of authority is transcript-only (6A 00:08:41).
168	- Diagnostic questions 1 to 3: PDF-confirmed (Workbook p.2). Question 4 (return-to-run model) transcript-only (6A 00:06:12).
169	- Failure Case reflection A to E: PDF-confirmed (Workbook p.1 to p.5).
170	- Discipline lens map and scenario pre-commitment: PDF-confirmed (Part A p.1). Grade 2A hamstring and day-by-day specifics transcript-only (6B 00:03:01).
171	- Technical challenge versus active resistance, SOPs as screening, first meetings matter: PDF-confirmed (Part A p.2). The unplanned eccentric test anecdote, the SEC identification and the first-meeting script wording are transcript-only (6B 00:07:17 to 00:12:02); the anecdote is Weber's account of causation, unverified.
172	- Bone stress confession: PDF-confirmed (Part A p.2); six-week, "not an MRI", coach-defers-to-doctor details transcript-only (6A 00:14:05; 6B 00:12:51).
173	- Translation as cognitive cost, education before translation, two routes, Option A / B, eccentric hamstring as divisive metric, pelvic control case: all PDF-confirmed (Part B p.1 to p.3).
174	- Six-stage pathway, five failure points, audit questions, 20-second rule, "advisory at best": transcript-only (6D); no PDF for this lab. Transcript quality is fair: "earn to play" is return to play, "force flight" is force plate, "SCMs" is unclear (possibly SEMs).
175	- Grey zone definition, K-B Matrix categories and combinations, one operational logic, phase ownership model, cross-check, empowerment checklist, communication framework, walkthrough, master checklist: PDF-confirmed (Grey Zone Workbook p.1 to p.12; Summary p.1 to p.8). The Summary attributes quotes to Dr Jason Weber by name.
176	- 10th Man, Devil's Advocate Unit, Six Hats, Pre-Mortem, System 1/2, Red Team questions, OODA, Bias Prompt Analysis and references: PDF-confirmed (Structured Thinking p.1 to p.8). Pre-mortem and red teaming as named protocols are PDF-only; the podcast covers 10th Man, Six Hats, Kahneman and OODA.
177	- Silent rugby coach, "five minutes data only", AFL calf case and doctor-as-messenger: transcript-only (Podcast 00:05:04 to 00:10:00). "Darren Burgess" and a "Two Coaches and a Coffee" podcast are plausible but unverified.
178	- Transcript term glossary: "dilutriate" = data literate; "SpeedCig" = SpeedSig (Weber's gait product, confirmed Structured Thinking p.1); "kyagi" = Kaigi; "Oodaloop" = OODA loop; "Module 60" = 6E; "stelitis" probably soleus; "conifiable" unclear (quantifiable or codifiable).
179	
180	## Applicability notes
181	
182	- The grey zone at Baylor is Athletic Medicine (athletic trainers, team physicians) to Athletic Performance, with Applied Performance on the data and analysis side of both. Weber's SEC example (new performance staff who share everything meeting incumbent medical staff who share nothing) is the closest case to a U.S. university structure, and his answer is a first-meeting operating statement plus written SOPs, not a turf negotiation. One adjustment: the team physician holds legal clearance authority in the college model, so the Rehab Phase Ownership Map should give Athletic Medicine the clearance gates at Return to Function and Return to Competition regardless of who owns operational progression in between.
183	- The Decision Empowerment Checklist and Communication Protocol are the fastest wins for athlete-availability decisions. Fill the seven-row empowerment table for one sport (who can pull an athlete from a field session, who can progress running exposure, what must reach the Director), then the five-row communication table with the head coach's notification path explicit and immediate. The course's line that a correct decision nobody communicated is a structural failure fits the football staff's sensitivity to seeing an athlete walk off the field.
184	- The six-stage Decision Pathway audit maps directly onto Applied Performance's pipeline (Catapult and force plate capture, quality control, thresholds, interpretation, coach-facing reporting). Run the dirty-data and expertise-gap questions (who owns QC, where were thresholds inherited from, is there a handover when staff change) on the current monitoring stack before the next staff transition, and adopt the 20-second recommendation-first rule as the standard for coach-facing reports.
185	- The Walkthrough Exercise is a ready-made agenda for an interdisciplinary return-to-play case review: one recent case, the athletic trainer and the performance coach each answer the six questions in front of each other, mark two or three divergence points, write the integration protocol for the top one. Once per semester with the current Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance pairing satisfies the "revisit after any staff change" rule.
186	- The One Operational Logic table is where the department decides in advance which data can trigger a unilateral decision and which need triangulation. For Baylor that means agreeing in writing where GPS exposure, force plate asymmetry, isometric strength and clinical assessment sit relative to each other in return to play, so a single metric or a dominant personality cannot impose its bias mid-pathway.
187	- Once Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance are aligned, the Bias Prompt Analysis is the counterweight. Before a return-to-play decision is logged, run the four layers and store the top two pre-mortem answers as review triggers. This gives Applied Performance a defined dissent role in the room that is procedural rather than personal.

# Module 4: The Integration Problem (Data to Decisions)

Numbering note: the course materials label this block internally as "Module 6" (Section 1 / 6A, 6B Part A and B, 6E, Podcast 6). The lecturer is Dr Jason Weber (Old Bull Performance). Eric's Drive folder calls it Module 4 and that number is used here. Where the video says "Module 6C" it is the file titled 6D The Decision Pathway; where it says "6B Part 2" it is 6C The Translation Problem.

The module's argument is that technically strong practitioners fail to influence decisions not because they lack knowledge but because the department has no operating model that carries information from collection to action. Weber names five places where that chain breaks (language, decision pathway, authority, relationship, process), then goes deeper on two of them: the encoding problem (each discipline reads the same athlete through a different lens) and the translation problem (someone is permanently re-explaining the basics, which is a leadership failure disguised as a communication chore). He then makes the pathway explicit as six stages with five audit points, and applies the whole thing to the physio to strength-and-conditioning overlap he calls the grey zone, which must be profiled, owned, gated and communicated rather than left to personality. The closing podcast argues that once a department is aligned, the new risk is groupthink, so leaders need structured dissent built into the decision log. The through-line is Weber's own confession: he had the right data on bone stress risk and the injuries he predicted happened anyway, because he had not made the information consumable to the doctor and the coach in advance.

## Lessons

### Video Lab 6A: The Integration Problem (15:42), with 6A Summary PDF, Integration Cheat Sheet PDF, Integration Problem Workbook PDF

- The failure mode: a data-literate, sharp practitioner whose recommendations are ignored, diluted or not understood. "It's typically not a knowledge problem, it's an integration problem" (00:01:00).
- Warning signs (00:01:20 to 00:04:22): no upward pathway; other departments do not understand you; junior staff unaware they are stage one of five; terminology confusion; a dismissive domain owner; philosophical differences in models.
- Four self-audit questions and five integration breakpoints (00:05:54 to 00:13:07); see Frameworks 1 and 2.
- On authority: make the call, but explain it in the meeting and again privately, and let the argument run rather than shutting it down (00:08:41 to 00:10:20).
- Weber's confession: bone stress data was not "medically friendly", the coach deferred to a doctor who did not understand it, and the predicted injuries arrived six weeks later (00:14:05 to 00:15:10).

### Video Lab 6B: The Encoding Problem (16:23), with Module_6B_Part_A PDF

- Disciplines encode the same facts differently: physio sees tissue tolerance, medical sees health risk, strength staff see outputs, sport science sees load, the coach sees availability. Nobody disagrees on the facts, only on what they mean (00:00:23 to 00:01:28; PDF p.1).
- Realigning the encoding framework is the core leadership job and requires written scenario pre-commitment ("when we get A, this is what we do"); see Framework 4.
- The health indicator of alignment: staff know what each other will do next, so nobody withholds an opinion or a handover (00:04:46 to 00:06:07; PDF p.1).
- Reasoned technical challenge is welcome; working outside the agreed process is not. The physio who ran an unplanned maximal eccentric test the day before a game, after which the player tore, is the cautionary case (00:06:38 to 00:09:31; PDF p.2).
- SOPs reveal who can operate inside a collaborative system; the SEC football example and first-meeting script are the model for inheriting a divided department (00:09:33 to 00:12:22; PDF p.2); see Framework 5.
- "As a technician I probably did a good job, but as a leader I didn't" (00:14:27): the doctor called the bone stress data "not an MRI".

### Video Lab 6C: The Translation Problem (13:04), with Module_6B_Part_B PDF

- Translation is the daily cost of unresolved encoding: explaining the same issue to medical, strength, physio, then coach. A "performance leak" (PDF p.1) and a threat to "cognitive survivability" (00:07:24).
- "Avoid translation, focus on education, and focus on it early" (00:02:25). Constant re-explanation is diagnostic evidence that the system is not aligned (PDF p.1).
- Two routes (line in the sand, or workshops and internal CPD) and the Option A / Option B leadership choice; see Framework 6.
- Contested metrics (eccentric hamstring is the example) need an agreed place in the framework before high-level meetings (00:06:12 to 00:07:21; PDF p.2).
- Worked case: pelvic control in stance was framed as a strength deficit; isometric abduction showed athletes were strong enough and the problem was motor control. A line in the sand drawn with evidence, not authority (00:08:30 to 00:10:58; PDF p.2 to p.3).

### Video Lab 6D: The Decision Pathway (12:14), no companion PDF

- Every significant decision travels six stages with five failure points between them, each with an audit question (00:01:06 to 00:10:50); see Framework 7.
- Communication example: "moderate signal, want to be cautious" lands with a coach as "no recommendation", when the practitioner meant "reduce intensity 15%" (00:06:27).
- The 20-second rule: lead with the recommendation, not the method or the number (00:07:46). Weber guards the channel between his level and the head coach (00:07:08).
- Authority example: physio recommends no contact, coach agrees, 20 minutes later the athlete is in full contact with no recorded override. Keep written notes (00:09:11 to 00:10:34).
- The highest-friction failure point is usually the one closest to stage six, where consequences are visible (00:11:09).

### Video Lab 6E: The Grey Zone (13:15), with Grey Zone Workbook PDF and Grey Zone Summary PDF

- The grey zone is where physio and strength staff work on the same athlete from different timelines, risk tolerances and definitions. It exists everywhere; the problem is it has not been structured, so people default to assumption (00:00:22 to 00:01:35; Summary p.1).
- People before process: profile everyone in the interface on the Knowledge-Behaviour Matrix, because the same model works with one pair and fails with another (00:02:44 to 00:03:59; Summary p.2).
- One operational logic, not medical and performance logics in parallel, agreed before measurement influences the pathway (00:03:59 to 00:05:28; Summary p.3).
- Phase ownership, empowerment levels and communication rules (00:05:34 to 00:10:43); "wearing the S&C badge" does not mean you can coach running; see Framework 8.
- The walkthrough exercise: tell one case twice, physio's eyes then S&C's, find the divergence points, write an integration protocol for each (00:10:43 to 00:12:12).

### Podcast 6: Structured Thinking Under Pressure (14:04), with Structured_Thinking_Under_Pressure PDF

- "Seeing around corners" requires stepping out of the processes you built (working on the business, not in it) and asking, bluntly, what could derail this (00:00:41 to 00:02:02).
- The 10th Man Rule from World War Z is dramatised but real (Israel's Devil's Advocate Unit, post-1973). Once everyone is "playing nicely in the sandpit", groupthink is the new risk (00:02:02 to 00:04:37; PDF p.1 to p.2).
- Most technology infers an outcome rather than measuring it; do not let the group agree its way past that (00:04:06).
- Meeting techniques: the rugby coach who sits silent then asks questions designed to unravel the plan; "five minutes, data only, no grand final pressure" (00:05:04 to 00:07:32).
- The AFL calf case: recurrent fatigue tears the coach understood intellectually but not emotionally; the fix was the doctor saying "stop everything", a different messenger for the same conclusion (00:08:04 to 00:10:00).
- A working system must be re-reviewed as staff, technology and knowledge change (00:11:57 to 00:13:42); see Framework 9.

## Frameworks and tools taught

### 1. The Five Integration Breakpoints (6A; Cheat Sheet p.1; Workbook p.4; 6A Summary p.1)

A diagnostic for any past decision where sound technical work did not change the outcome. Tick which broke: (1) Language gap: no shared framework for status, readiness or risk, including philosophical gaps where the words are understood but the models differ. (2) Decision pathway gap: no pre-agreed route for who collects, who reviews, where it goes next, what triggers a conversation. (3) Authority gradient: a senior figure overrides sound input without challenge or explanation. (4) Relationship deficit: the decision maker does not trust or understand the source; Weber treats this as the practitioner's responsibility to pre-educate. (5) Process absence: no meeting, gate or checkpoint requires the input to be addressed before the decision is finalised. Product: a named breakpoint for a specific case, plus what would have needed to be different.

### 2. The Diagnostic Questions (Workbook p.2; 6A 00:05:54)

Ask of yourself or each staff member: (1) When did your data last directly change a coaching decision? If none in three months, that is the answer. Trace the pathway. (2) How many people could accurately explain what the monitoring system measures and why? Estimate, name the gaps by role, state the cost. (3) What happens to your recommendations when you are not in the room: hold, modified, or disappear? (4, video only) How many could explain the return-to-run model and its decision gates?

### 3. The Real-World Failure Case reflection (Integration Workbook p.1 to p.5)

Sections A to E in order. A: define the integration problem as it appears in your environment; rate frequency (rarely / occasionally / regularly / almost always) and describe one observable signal. C: one case where technical quality was sound but the process produced a poor outcome: context and people; what the data indicated; what was decided instead and what overrode it; downstream cost to athlete, team, credibility, department. Optional table for multiple cases (Situation / What the data said / What happened instead / Downstream cost). D: locate the break against the five breakpoints; one-off or recurring and what has blocked resolution; what would have needed to be different (a process, relationship, language, structure or moment). E: complete "The one integration failure in my current environment that I most need to resolve is..." and bring it to the live session. The workbook states the rest of the module is built as responses to this case.

### 4. Encoding Realignment by scenario pre-commitment (6B; Part A PDF p.1)

Pick a common presentation (Weber uses a grade 2A hamstring). Before it happens, with every discipline in the room, write: how it will be assessed; the checkpoints; day-by-day expectations and tempo; the realistic return-to-performance timeline; who acts at each handover (for example day four to running staff); criteria for adapting off the plan. The output is a document the staff built together, which is what the coach sees ("this is the plan, these are the checkpoints"), and which is the reference for judging whether a deviation is a reasoned challenge or someone working outside the system. Repeat for performance progressions. Health check: can the physio describe what the strength coach will do next week, and vice versa.

### 5. First-meeting operating statement and SOPs (6B 00:11:43 to 00:12:22; Part A PDF p.2)

When inheriting a department, the first group meeting sets the encoding framework: who you are, what you do, how the department will operate, that you were hired to install a system rather than remove people, and that everyone will work to it. SOPs follow and are positioned as the way to find out who can work inside a collaborative system, and the transparent basis for escalating anyone who cannot.

### 6. The Translation Audit and the Option A / Option B choice (6C; Part B PDF p.1 to p.2)

List every concept you re-explain to a second and third audience in the same week; each is a gap. For each gap choose the route: line in the sand or education through workshops and internal CPD. Decide honestly who teaches it: Option A, you have the technical depth and stand up and explain the framework; Option B, you hire or empower the person who does and trust them, and do not defer to someone because it is easy. Agree in advance how contested metrics are framed in this environment. Product: an education plan sized to the resources you actually have.

### 7. The Six-Stage Decision Pathway and Five-Point Audit (6D, transcript only)

Stages: (1) data capture: GPS, force plate, RPE, clinical assessment, observation; (2) quality control: protocol followed, conditions consistent, anomalies caught; (3) analysis: thresholds, baselines; (4) interpretation: this number means the athlete is in this state; (5) communication: presenting to the person who acts; (6) decision and action.

Failure points and audit questions:

1. Dirty data (between 1 and 2). Unit not worn correctly, plate not zeroed, protocol skipped, and it sits in the database for weeks. Ask: who owns quality control and what does the check specifically consist of? If the answer is "nobody, it's informal", that is the finding.
2. Expertise gap (between 2 and 3). Data reliable but the analyst lacks the framework: normal-limit changes flagged as severe, a 50 ms RFD change on shoulder external rotation treated as an emergency. Ask: who set the thresholds, where were the defaults inherited from, is it written in a software platform, who reviews it, and is there a high-clarity handover when staff change?
3. Interpretation gap (between 3 and 4). A number is reported and the meeting moves on. Often caused by collecting more than the system can process. Ask: does it stop at the number, and who is there to handle it?
4. Communication gap (between 4 and 5). Technically precise, operationally opaque. Ask: what do you lead with, the method, the number or the recommendation? Apply the 20-second rule and a pre-built delivery structure for the coach.
5. Authority gap (between 5 and 6). Clear recommendation, no gate, never becomes a decision. Ask: is there a pre-agreed process that requires technical input to be formally addressed before return to play or selection is finalised? If not, recommendations are "advisory at best, optional at worst".

Product: name the single failure point costing the most decision quality each week (not the one that implicates someone) and fix it first. Keep written notes on every recommendation and decision.

### 8. The Grey Zone build, seven steps (6E; Grey Zone Workbook p.1 to p.12; Grey Zone Summary p.2 to p.7)

Run in order; the diagnostic leads into the design, which leads into the operating protocols.

Step 1, People Profile (Workbook p.2 to p.3). Map every staff member in the physio-S&C interface: Knowledge level (Handbrake: low knowledge, defaults to assumption, needs close supervision; Pawn: has knowledge but relies on instruction, hesitates at transitions; Practitioner: competent in own domain, collaboration depends on openness; Operator: high knowledge, autonomous, check for territorial bias) crossed with Behaviour (Misaligned: works against departmental logic; Coaster: present but passive under pressure; Catalyst: drives collaboration, anchor your protocols here; Beacon: sets the standard, amplifies or, if misaligned, undermines). Combinations needing extra structure: Misaligned x Operator; Beacon (Misaligned) x any Handbrake; two Practitioners with different domain biases; Pawn S&C + Operator Physio. Combinations that self-organise: Beacon x Catalyst; Operator x Operator with explicit handover points; Catalyst x Practitioner. Write the biggest risk in this specific pairing and the level of structure it needs.

Step 2, One Operational Logic (Workbook p.4; Summary p.3). Facilitate and record the agreed position (not individual opinions) on six domains: hamstring rehab markers; running readiness criteria (quality of movement versus quantity of exposure); return to full training threshold (what tests, who signs off); data we trust in-house; data we do not act on in isolation; what "athlete ready" means. Leave a row blank if unresolved; the blank is the priority.

Step 3, Rehab Phase Ownership Map (Workbook p.5; Summary p.4). For Return to Function (acute / post-surgical), Return to Run (loading), Return to Play (performance rebuild), Return to Competition: who owns it, who contributes, transition criteria, escalation required. Weber's reference: medical/physio owns RTF with S&C running parallel conditioning ("physio controls direction, S&C does not wait"); S&C owns RTR in most environments unless an exceptional running physio changes the calculus; RTP shared per pre-agreed criteria; RTC department-lead sign-off with immediate communication to the head coach. Pre-agree before any athlete is injured.

Step 4, Cross-Check Method (6E 00:07:43; Summary p.4). Even when S&C owns the phase, ask the physio to account for it. If the physio can relay the rationale, communication happened; if not, it did not. This is how you verify the model is running rather than assumed.

Step 5, Decision Empowerment Checklist (Workbook p.6; Summary p.5). For seven decision types (progress loading within agreed programme; regress loading; remove athlete from a field session; modify a published session; progress to next rehab phase; seek external specialist referral; return athlete to full contact) mark Yes/No for physio can act, S&C can act, must escalate to department lead. Skipping this produces overreach (Operator knowledge without role boundaries) or paralysis (Pawn behaviour in a Practitioner role, holding athletes back waiting for permission never withheld).

Step 6, Communication Protocol (Workbook p.7; Summary p.5 to p.6). For each decision event (athlete removed from field session; phase progressed; phase regressed or paused; specialist referral; return to full training cleared) fill in who is told, how fast, via what channel. Rules: the operationally responsible person owns the communication; the list is pre-defined per decision type; anything touching field presence is immediate, not end of session, not email; escalation triggers are pre-agreed so escalation is never a surprise. Then write the single biggest communication failure point and the one protocol change that fixes it.

Step 7, Walkthrough Exercise (Workbook p.8 to p.9; Summary p.6 to p.7). Choose one real or well-built hypothetical case. Physio and S&C coach each answer, in front of each other: what does progress look like; key risks right now; what data do you trust; time constraints; where do you need the other discipline most; what would cause you to pause or regress. Mark two or three divergence points. For the top one write the integration protocol: who owns this moment; what criteria determine the outcome; what is handed over and to whom; who can change the programme; who must be informed; what goes to the department lead without exception.

Finish with the Grey Zone Master Checklist (Workbook p.10 to p.11): 22 boxes across People Diagnosis, Operational Logic, Phase Ownership, Decision Empowerment, Communication, Ongoing Operations. "A blank box is a structural risk." Re-run after any staff change or mid-season.

### 9. Structured dissent toolkit (Podcast 6; Structured Thinking PDF p.1 to p.8)

- 10th Man Rule: when consensus forms, one person has the formal, protected obligation to argue the opposite. OBP application: designate that voice in the Kaigi decision log before RTR or programme calls are logged (PDF p.6).
- Six Thinking Hats (de Bono): White facts only; Red gut feel without justification; Black what could go wrong (the 10th Man hat); Yellow best case; Green alternative paths; Blue process control, who owns the decision and what is the review trigger. Everyone wears the same hat at the same time (PDF p.2 to p.3). Weber's lightweight version: "five minutes, data only".
- Pre-Mortem (Klein / Kahneman), three steps: state the decision; project forward ("it is four weeks from now, he is re-injured, what happened?") with each person writing independently before discussion; collect and group the failure scenarios and use the most credible to add contingencies before committing (PDF p.3).
- System 1 / System 2: Go/No-Go and Kaigi exist to force slow thinking onto decisions staff would otherwise make on pattern recognition, especially when a situation looks familiar but is not (PDF p.4).
- Red Teaming, five questions: under what conditions does this monitoring system give false confidence; what would have to be true about this athlete for our RTR assessment to be wrong; where are we relying on a single source; what are we not measuring and does the decision assume it is fine; if a different department looked at this data what would they conclude. Inter-departmental version: medical reviews performance decisions, S&C stress-tests medical thresholds (PDF p.4 to p.6).
- OODA loop: orientation (the department's "concept") is the underrated failure stage; accurate data through a stale filter still gives a wrong decision. Ask when you last reoriented your monitoring assumptions (PDF p.5 to p.6).
- OBP Bias Prompt Analysis, four layers to run before a decision is logged (PDF p.6 to p.7): (1) Recognition: what do we know, facts only; (2) Assumption audit: what are we treating as stable that might not be, when did we last check our concept; (3) Inversion: assign a 10th Man to argue the opposite and record the argument; (4) Pre-mortem close: "if this decision is wrong in four weeks, what happened?", record the top two answers in the decision log as review triggers.

## Deliverables / exercises

1. Integration Problem Workbook (5 pages): sections A to E per Framework 3, ending with the one-sentence closing statement for the live session.
2. Translation gap identification: 6C (00:02:31) refers to "the workbook associated with this lab". No such workbook is in the course folder; the Part B PDF is prose. Framework 6 is the reconstruction.
3. Decision Pathway audit (6D, 00:10:52 to 00:12:11): trace one recent important decision through all six stages, name the costliest failure point, assign an owner and a specific check. No PDF accompanies this lab.
4. Grey Zone Workbook (12 pages): People Profile and combination check (p.3); Operational Logic table (p.4); Rehab Phase Ownership Map (p.5); Decision Empowerment Checklist (p.6); Communication Protocol (p.7); Walkthrough table and divergence points (p.8 to p.9); Master Checklist (p.10 to p.11). Complete the People Profile first; design for the real environment; revisit after any staff change.
5. Structured Thinking: watch World War Z as a priming device (podcast 00:13:36; PDF p.6), then run the four-layer Bias Prompt Analysis on a live return-to-play or programme decision and record the review triggers. The PDF closes with: what is your department's current concept, when did you last audit it, how old is the filter you run monitoring data through (p.8).

## Key quotes

- "It's typically not a knowledge problem. It's an integration problem." (6A, 00:01:00)
- "It's not just about what I can do. It's about what I can get my team to do." (6A, 00:11:59)
- "If your recommendation changes as it moves up the chain, there is likely an integration leak." (Integration Cheat Sheet, p.1)
- "As a technician, I probably did a good job, but as a leader, I didn't." (6B, 00:14:27)
- "Translation is not just inconvenient. It is a performance leak inside the organisation." (Module 6B Part B PDF, p.1)
- "If you're more than 20 seconds away from getting an actual recommendation or coach, it's going to be lost." (6D, 00:07:56; transcript wording)
- "Otherwise, recommendations become advisory at best and optional at worst." (6D, 00:10:43)
- "The gray zone is not something we eliminate. It's something we organise." (6E, 00:12:16; also Grey Zone Workbook p.1)
- "Unowned zones always fill with assumption." (Grey Zone Workbook, p.12)
- "Don't wait for someone brave enough to raise the concern. Build the mechanism that makes raising it expected, protected, and logged." (Structured Thinking PDF, p.7)

## Source confidence

PDF extraction: all eight PDFs yielded full text (pypdf). None were image-only. The Grey Zone Workbook (12 pages) was additionally read as page images because of the Read tool's 10-page limit; its text layer also extracted cleanly, so page references are reliable.

| PDF | Pages | Text extracted |
|---|---|---|
| The_Leader_s_Integration_Cheat_Sheet.pdf | 1 | Yes |
| The_Integration_Problem_Workbook.pdf | 5 | Yes |
| Video_Lab_6A_Summary_-_The_Integration_Problem.pdf | 1 | Yes |
| Module_6B_Part_A_-_The_Encoding_Problem.pdf | 3 | Yes |
| Module_6B_Part_B_-_The_Translation_Problem.pdf | 3 | Yes |
| Structured_Thinking_Under_Pressure.pdf | 8 | Yes |
| The_Grey_Zone_Workbook.pdf | 12 | Yes (also read as images) |
| Video_Lab_The_Grey_Zone_Summary.pdf | 8 | Yes |

By framework:

- Five breakpoints: PDF-confirmed (Cheat Sheet p.1; Workbook p.4; 6A Summary p.1). The explain-in-meeting-and-again-privately handling of authority is transcript-only (6A 00:08:41).
- Diagnostic questions 1 to 3: PDF-confirmed (Workbook p.2). Question 4 (return-to-run model) transcript-only (6A 00:06:12).
- Failure Case reflection A to E: PDF-confirmed (Workbook p.1 to p.5).
- Discipline lens map and scenario pre-commitment: PDF-confirmed (Part A p.1). Grade 2A hamstring and day-by-day specifics transcript-only (6B 00:03:01).
- Technical challenge versus active resistance, SOPs as screening, first meetings matter: PDF-confirmed (Part A p.2). The unplanned eccentric test anecdote, the SEC identification and the first-meeting script wording are transcript-only (6B 00:07:17 to 00:12:02); the anecdote is Weber's account of causation, unverified.
- Bone stress confession: PDF-confirmed (Part A p.2); six-week, "not an MRI", coach-defers-to-doctor details transcript-only (6A 00:14:05; 6B 00:12:51).
- Translation as cognitive cost, education before translation, two routes, Option A / B, eccentric hamstring as divisive metric, pelvic control case: all PDF-confirmed (Part B p.1 to p.3).
- Six-stage pathway, five failure points, audit questions, 20-second rule, "advisory at best": transcript-only (6D); no PDF for this lab. Transcript quality is fair: "earn to play" is return to play, "force flight" is force plate, "SCMs" is unclear (possibly SEMs).
- Grey zone definition, K-B Matrix categories and combinations, one operational logic, phase ownership model, cross-check, empowerment checklist, communication framework, walkthrough, master checklist: PDF-confirmed (Grey Zone Workbook p.1 to p.12; Summary p.1 to p.8). The Summary attributes quotes to Dr Jason Weber by name.
- 10th Man, Devil's Advocate Unit, Six Hats, Pre-Mortem, System 1/2, Red Team questions, OODA, Bias Prompt Analysis and references: PDF-confirmed (Structured Thinking p.1 to p.8). Pre-mortem and red teaming as named protocols are PDF-only; the podcast covers 10th Man, Six Hats, Kahneman and OODA.
- Silent rugby coach, "five minutes data only", AFL calf case and doctor-as-messenger: transcript-only (Podcast 00:05:04 to 00:10:00). "Darren Burgess" and a "Two Coaches and a Coffee" podcast are plausible but unverified.
- Transcript term glossary: "dilutriate" = data literate; "SpeedCig" = SpeedSig (Weber's gait product, confirmed Structured Thinking p.1); "kyagi" = Kaigi; "Oodaloop" = OODA loop; "Module 60" = 6E; "stelitis" probably soleus; "conifiable" unclear (quantifiable or codifiable).

## Applicability notes

- The grey zone at Baylor is Athletic Medicine (athletic trainers, team physicians) to Athletic Performance, with Applied Performance on the data and analysis side of both. Weber's SEC example (new performance staff who share everything meeting incumbent medical staff who share nothing) is the closest case to a U.S. university structure, and his answer is a first-meeting operating statement plus written SOPs, not a turf negotiation. One adjustment: the team physician holds legal clearance authority in the college model, so the Rehab Phase Ownership Map should give Athletic Medicine the clearance gates at Return to Function and Return to Competition regardless of who owns operational progression in between.
- The Decision Empowerment Checklist and Communication Protocol are the fastest wins for athlete-availability decisions. Fill the seven-row empowerment table for one sport (who can pull an athlete from a field session, who can progress running exposure, what must reach the Director), then the five-row communication table with the head coach's notification path explicit and immediate. The course's line that a correct decision nobody communicated is a structural failure fits the football staff's sensitivity to seeing an athlete walk off the field.
- The six-stage Decision Pathway audit maps directly onto Applied Performance's pipeline (Catapult and force plate capture, quality control, thresholds, interpretation, coach-facing reporting). Run the dirty-data and expertise-gap questions (who owns QC, where were thresholds inherited from, is there a handover when staff change) on the current monitoring stack before the next staff transition, and adopt the 20-second recommendation-first rule as the standard for coach-facing reports.
- The Walkthrough Exercise is a ready-made agenda for an interdisciplinary return-to-play case review: one recent case, the athletic trainer and the performance coach each answer the six questions in front of each other, mark two or three divergence points, write the integration protocol for the top one. Once per semester with the current Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance pairing satisfies the "revisit after any staff change" rule.
- The One Operational Logic table is where the department decides in advance which data can trigger a unilateral decision and which need triangulation. For Baylor that means agreeing in writing where GPS exposure, force plate asymmetry, isometric strength and clinical assessment sit relative to each other in return to play, so a single metric or a dominant personality cannot impose its bias mid-pathway.
- Once Athletic Medicine and Athletic Performance are aligned, the Bias Prompt Analysis is the counterweight. Before a return-to-play decision is logged, run the four layers and store the top two pre-mortem answers as review triggers. This gives Applied Performance a defined dissent role in the room that is procedural rather than personal.

# Eric Rash context brief (for staff-development and department-building recommendations)

Compiled 2026-09-24 from the DEV workspace, the SecondBrain vault, and Claude memory. Read-only pass; nothing else was modified. Sources are date-stamped in section 8 because they span June to September 2026 and some are stale. Anything not stated in a source is marked (inferred). No athlete names or athlete health information appear here by design.

Naming rule for anything staff-facing that comes out of this: Athletic Performance (not S&C), Athletic Medicine (not sports medicine), Applied Performance (not sport science).

## Role and remit

- Title: Director of Applied Performance, Baylor University Athletics. About eight years in the department, promoted into the director seat from within. Source: `ContextVault/Career-Context-Document.md` (2026-06-08).
- Where the unit sits: Applied Performance is a support and enablement function inside Health & Wellness, behind the athlete-facing units (Athletic Medicine, Athletic Performance, Mental Health, Performance Nutrition). It is not athlete-facing itself. Source: Career-Context-Document; `Education_Alignment_Initiative/docs/context.md`.
- Reporting line: formal supervisor is Chris Ruf, Director of Athletic Performance, since a 2025 reporting change that moved Eric off administrative senior staff (where he reported to Kenny Boyd, Executive Senior Associate AD). The June career document records that the change cost him access to Kenny and senior conversations. Since then: the July 2026 responsibilities document came from Chris and Kenny jointly, the biweekly status report goes to both, and in August Kenny named Eric the Athletics point of contact to ITS. Some access to Kenny has been rebuilt through the JD process and the technology work (inferred). Chris prefers email. Sources: Career-Context-Document; `KeystoneOS memory project-jd-okr-2026.md`; `SoftwareTech_Mgmt_Framework/docs/MICAH_MEETING_REQUEST_2026-08-13.md`; `BAIR_Steering_Committee/docs/context.md` (which lists Kenny as the person Eric reports to; treat as the BAIR-lane relationship, not the formal line).
- The July 2026 JD shifted the role from doer to director. It names: department oversight, BAIR Steering Committee oversight and organization, HPI (human performance integration) protocols, technology vetting, vendor relations and onboarding, data infrastructure, guidance to Health & Wellness staff on technology and data, and Spirit Squad as a direct team-training responsibility. Source: `project-jd-okr-2026.md`; `SecondBrain/Projects/Applied-Performance-JD-2026/decisions.md` (2026-07-17).
- Three permanent service pillars in the current OKR structure (v3): Data Systems & Analytics, Education, Research & Development, plus an enabling objective, Leadership & Visibility. Mission sentence used in briefings: "Applied Performance turns Baylor's athlete data into decisions that keep athletes available and performing." North star: be the best applied performance department in the country. Source: `SecondBrain/Projects/Applied-Performance-OKRs-2026-27.md` (v3, Fall set authored 2026-09-14).
- Eric's protected hands-on lanes (not delegated): HPI protocol and its dashboarding; technology vetting; white-paper analysis; one-off reports and dashboards for sports. Delegation stops at those boundaries. Source: OKR doc v3.
- Decision rights (June 2026 read): owns what projects to pursue, what questions to chase, how to source data, and can take a meeting with almost anyone on campus. Needs Chris for spending and hiring. No budget line. No control over whether other units adopt his work. The JD clarifying questions (July) show that authority thresholds, budget, evaluation of staff, and escalation were still undefined at that point. Sources: Career-Context-Document; `SecondBrain/Projects/Applied-Performance-JD-2026/JD-clarifying-questions.md`.
- Accountability: Eric authors his own OKRs; no one external holds him to them. The v3 system adds self-imposed teeth: semester cycles, an Oct 15 mid-semester checkpoint, a Dec 18 close, and a timer-checked project slate. Source: OKR doc v3; `SecondBrain/Projects/Applied-Performance-Operating-Cadence.md` (2026-09-14).

## Staff and structure

Applied Performance unit (as of the v3 OKR doc and the 2026-08-24 supervisor update):

- Eric Rash, Director. Presents solo in briefings; staff appear on the org and lanes slide.
- AJ Tademy, Applied Performance Specialist, Football. Full-time. Owns football day-to-day: fall-camp planning, the practice-load framework (FaceComps color-coded day system and rep-count load model), the plan-vs-actual review to the football staff, and all football staff communications. JD relationship verb: Oversee. Concretely that means a weekly 1:1, Eric reviews any artifact before it leaves the department, and Eric stays out of daily operations. Summer KR 4.2 (AJ full handoff through fall camp) scored 1.0, so the handoff worked. Strength on record: ready to run the lane; the framework was jointly presented to staff before handoff. Gap: none stated in sources. Sources: OKR doc v3; `decisions.md` 0004; `JD-2026/CONTEXT.md`.
- Noah, Basketball Applied Performance GA. JD relationship verb: Support and guide (mentoring-weighted oversight; Eric teaches procedures, policies and data-management practice; Noah executes "with training wheels on"; Eric remains accountable for outcomes). Summer KR 4.3 (onboarding checklist plus weekly 1:1) scored 0.0. Fall KR 4.2 is a Noah 1:1 every two weeks. Open question to Chris: whether the basketball position is permanent, renewable, or disappears when the GA term ends. Sources: OKR doc v3; CONTEXT.md; JD-clarifying-questions.
- Linda. Role under Applied Performance is still being defined. Leadership stated Eric's role toward her is supportive, not directive. Eric met with her twice in August and they listed four potential projects supporting Tennis and Athletic Performance. A `DEV/Linda Projects` folder exists. Sources: `Supervisor_Reviews/updates/Bi-Weekly_Update_2026-08-24.md`; decisions.md 0003; DEV `CLAUDE.md` and `PROGRAM.md`.
- Blake Wright, PhD fellow, has left the organization (established 2026-07-17). He is removed from all forward planning; his KR co-ownership was redistributed to Eric and AJ; the white paper is now Eric's sole critical path with Blake credited as co-author. Several older sources still list him as current (the Applied-Performance-Hub dated 2026-06-01, the BAIR context, the okr-staff-meeting-prep memory). Treat those as stale. Source: decisions.md 0003 and 0005.
- Student workers: the 08-24 update says "whatever student workers we have." No names, count, or scope anywhere in the sources.
- Interns: an intern program exists as a concept with a curriculum design and SOP templates, but there is no evidence in the sources of a current intern cohort. See section 3.

Adjacent groups and named contacts (staff only):

entries.description:
Run multiple commands in ONE call. Every command's output is auto-indexed into the knowledge base; if you also pass `queries`, the matching sections come back in the same round trip so a follow-up search call is not needed.

Concurrency parallelizes the FETCH phase (run-the-commands). The DERIVATION phase — turning raw output into an answer — still belongs in code: add a processing command that consumes the indexed output and prints only the answer, so the raw bytes never enter your conversation (Think-in-Code, same principle as the sandbox tool).

WHEN:
  - You have 3+ related commands you would otherwise run sequentially (multi-issue lookups, git log + git diff + git blame, multi-file reads, multi-region cloud queries)
  - You want to gather AND query in one round trip — pass `queries` so the matching sections come back inline
  - You want to parallelize I/O-bound work — pass `concurrency` 2-8 (network calls, gh CLI, cloud APIs, multi-repo git reads)
  - The combined output is large enough that piping it through ctx_search later would itself be expensive — let auto-index + inline queries do both in one shot

WHEN NOT:
  - Single command with no follow-up query — run it in the sandbox tool directly
  - CPU-bound or stateful commands — keep concurrency at 1 (npm test, build, lint, port-binding servers, lock-file holders, anything that races on the same resource)

RETURNS:
  Auto-indexed section list per command label, plus top matches per query (when `queries` is passed). Raw output is NOT echoed in full — only the matched windows. Concurrency>1 switches each command to its own per-command timeout (no shared budget); concurrency=1 preserves the legacy shared-budget cascading-skip-on-timeout path. Use 4-8 for I/O-bound batches; keep at 1 for CPU work or shared-state commands; lower the value when target hosts enforce per-IP rate limits.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search
entries.description:
Search a unified knowledge base with a multi-strategy ranking pipeline. Two parallel matchers run on every query: a Porter-stemming matcher ("caching" finds "cached", "caches", "cach") and a trigram-substring matcher ("useEff" finds "useEffect"). Their ranked lists are merged via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, so a document that ranks well in both surfaces above one that wins only on a single strategy. Multi-term queries get an additional proximity-rerank pass that boosts passages where the query terms appear close together. Typos are corrected via Levenshtein distance and re-searched. Result snippets are window-extracted around the matched terms, not blindly truncated.

The knowledge base is unified: queries reach indexed content you stored (ctx_index, ctx_fetch_and_index, ctx_batch_execute output) AND auto-captured session memory written by hooks (decisions, errors, blockers, plans, user prompts, rejected approaches, tool failures, compaction guides — 26 event categories). GRAMMAR SYNTAX:
- keyword:"search term" - Search for keywords in the content. If no scope is specified, the default scope is 'all'.
- scope:title|sentences|all - Define the search scope. Options are 'title', 'sentences', or 'all'. The default is 'all'.
- from:YYYY-MM-DD - Filter meetings from this date (ISO format)
- to:YYYY-MM-DD - Filter meetings until this date (ISO format)
- limit:N - Limit results (max 50)
- skip:N - Skip N results for pagination
- organizers:email1@x.com,email2@x.com - Filter by organizer emails (comma-separated)
- participants:email1@x.com,email2@x.com - Filter by participant emails (comma-separated)
- mine:true|false - Filter to only include user's own meetings
- channel:CHANNEL_ID - Filter meetings by channel/folder ID (use fireflies_list_channels() to find channel IDs)

EXAMPLES:
- "engineering standup" (simple keyword search)
- "keyword:\"performance\" scope:sentences limit:20"

import os, json, re, sys, urllib.request

key = os.environ["FIREFLIES_API_KEY"]
tid = "01KYQ91VD4Q2Q0DDZWVEBFRYKX"
q = {"query": '{ transcript(id: "%s") { title sentences { index speaker_name text start_time } } }' % tid}
req = urllib.request.Request("https://api.fireflies.ai/graphql", data=json.dumps(q).encode(),
                             headers={"Content-Type": "application/json", "Authorization": "Bearer " + key})
data = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=60))
s = data["data"]["transcript"]["sentences"]
print("sentences:", len(s))
kw = re.compile(r"care team|sport administrator|confidential|athletic health|health ?care advisory|advisory group|"
                r"software|data privacy|legal|teamworks|applied performance|sport science|performance staff|"
                r"strength|athletic train|athletic medicine|nutrition|mental health integration|senior associate|"
                r"restructur|reorgan|reporting|report to|unit report|staff folder|availability hours|documentation",
                re.I)
hits = [i for i, x in enumerate(s) if kw.search(x["text"] or "")]
print("hits:", len(hits))
# merge windows of +-1 sentence
windows = []
for i in hits:
    lo, hi = max(0, i - 1), min(len(s) - 1, i + 1)
    if windows and lo <= windows[-1][1] + 1:
        windows[-1][1] = hi
    else:
        windows.append([lo, hi])
def ts(t):
    t = int(t); return "%02d:%02d:%02d" % (t // 3600, (t % 3600) // 60, t % 60)
out = 0
for lo, hi in windows:
    txt = " ".join((x["text"] or "").strip() for x in s[lo:hi + 1])
    line = "[%s] %s: %s" % (ts(s[lo]["start_time"]), s[lo]["speaker_name"], txt)
    print(line[:700])
    out += 1
    if out > 220:
        print("...truncated"); break

# What this material is

"Running The Room" is a paid online course from Old Bull Performance, written and presented by Dr Jason Weber (former AFL high-performance manager, creator of the SpeedSig gait product). It is aimed at people who lead or want to lead a high-performance department: the physio, strength, sport-science and medical staff around a team. The material is 31 lessons (webinars, short video labs, three podcasts) and 26 PDFs (blogs, cheat sheets, worksheets, workbooks) across four modules. The course files label the fourth block "Module 6"; the Drive folder and these notes call it Module 4.

The argument across all four modules is one sentence: departments buy technology faster than they build the people, language and procedures needed to turn it into decisions, and the fix is discipline written down.

## The four modules

- **Module 1, People, language and discipline before technology.** Audit staff on a knowledge and behaviour grid, agree a common language (means before modality before technology, a shared athlete map), and inventory the tech stack by what it measures, not by brand.
- **Module 2, Turning technology into defensible decisions.** Separate measurement from inference, map every tool to the question it answers and the person who owns each step, decide whether a metric is monitored or tested, pre-agree decision gates, and quantify noise so the gates hold.
- **Module 3, Discipline equals freedom.** Meeting problems are meeting-type problems: name the modality (Decide, Diagnose, Inform, Build), time-box, pre-read, log every decision with an owner and a review date, and use meetings as leadership reps for staff.
- **Module 4, The integration problem.** Good technical work fails at five breakpoints (language, pathway, authority, relationship, process); structure the physio to strength grey zone with ownership, empowerment and communication rules; build dissent into the decision log.

## Tools worth keeping

| Tool | Where |
| --- | --- |
| Knowledge-Behaviour Matrix and Student Workbook | module-1 note; Lab_1b_Blog pp.1-3; Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook pp.1-5 |
| Means, modality, technology ordering and the CM² athlete map | module-1 note; Lab_1A_Blog pp.1-3 |
| Tech Stack Reality Check (inventory, reliability, one-page procedure) | module-1 note; Lab_1c_Tech_Stack_Audit pp.1-4 |
| Measured, inferred, probability, next step communication | module-2 note; Lab_2a pp.3-4 |
| Capability and Workflow Matrix | module-2 note; Lab_2b pp.2-3 |
| Monitoring vs testing rule and the five coach questions | module-2 note; Lab_2c pp.1-2 |
| Five-part decision gate and the MDC95 / SWC decision logic | module-2 note; Lab_2D pp.1-2; Lab_2E pp.1-2 |
| Meeting typology cheat sheet, Kaigi, Stoplight slide, decision log | module-3 note; Lab_3b cheat sheet pp.1-2; Lab_3a pp.1-3; Lab_3c template pp.1-2 |
| Lab 3D worksheet (meetings as staff development reps) | module-3 note; Lab_3D_Worksheet pp.1-3 |
| Grey Zone Workbook (people profile, operational logic, phase ownership, empowerment checklist, communication protocol) | module-4 note; The_Grey_Zone_Workbook pp.2-11 |
| Six-check evidence stack and the Bias Prompt Analysis | module-2 note; Stacking_Evidence pp.2-4; module-4 note; Structured_Thinking pp.6-7 |

## Caveat on sources

The lesson transcripts are unverified faster-whisper drafts with frequent mis-hearings (product names, statistics terms, the word Kaigi). The PDFs are the authoritative source and are cited by page wherever a claim rests on them. Anything marked transcript-only in the module notes (the six-stage decision pathway, the Webinar 3 operating practices, the pre-training go/no-go run order, the 20-minute meeting rules) is the speaker's spoken account with no written backup. The course media and PDFs stay on Drive and are never committed to this repo.
